documents.abstract: Abstract Last-mile delivery has emerged as a critical component of modern supply chain management due to the rapid growth of e-commerce, increasing customer expectations, and the need for faster and more reliable deliveries. Despite covering a relatively short distance, it is often one of the most complex and expensive stages of logistics, involving challenges related to route optimization, delivery costs, traffic congestion, environmental sustainability, and customer satisfaction. This study examines the evolution of last-mile delivery research from 2013 to 2026 using a bibliometric analysis of 2,771 journal publications retrieved from the Scopus database. The data was screened using the PRISMA approach and analysed using Biblioshiny to identify publication trends, influential journals, leading countries, research themes, keyword patterns, and citation impact across pre-COVID, pandemic, and post-COVID periods. The findings reveal a substantial increase in scientific publications, with research activity accelerating during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. China emerged as the leading contributor to publications by 2025, while India demonstrated significant growth in research output. Key themes have evolved from traditional city logistics and home delivery towards vehicle routing optimization, drone delivery, machine learning, parcel lockers, crowdshipping, and sustainable transportation. However, the study identifies important research gaps, including the limited use of real-world operational data, the need to balance cost efficiency with service quality and environmental sustainability, and the early-stage application of artificial intelligence and machine learning in delivery optimization. The study concludes that future research should focus on validating optimization models under actual operating conditions and developing integrated, data-driven solutions for more efficient and sustainable last-mile delivery systems. Keywords: Last-mile delivery, Operations Research, Bibliometric Analysis, Route Optimization, E-commerce, Drone Delivery, Machine Learning, Sustainability, Scopus, COVID-19.

Position paper with no original experiments. It closely reads five recent edge-cloud LLM inference papers and finds that evaluations often rely on idealized networks, synthetic workloads and averages instead of tail latency, and that none reports monetary cost or tests handover. It proposes a 13-row reporting checklist and two low-cost student mini projects.

The widespread deployment of foundational Large Language Models (LLM) across cloud datacenters marks a fundamental paradigm shift from stateless deep learning toward distributed, memory-intensive generative workloads. However, serving massive foundation models under stringent Service Level Objectives (SLO) exposes critical physical and system bottlenecks. These challenges include the persistent High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) wall, operational asymmetry between compute-bound prefilling and memory-bandwidth-bound decoding, explosive Key-Value (KV) cache expansion, prohibitive serverless cold starts, and hardware reliability vulnerabilities. Existing literature reviews remain layer-siloed, decoupling low-level accelerator virtualization from cluster orchestration and runtime inference, while largely overlooking defining advancements from 2024 to 2026. To address these limitations, this study presents a comprehensive, cross-layer systematic review guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 framework. We synthesize a holistic taxonomy unifying hardware virtualization, cluster-level scheduling, and runtime inference optimizations, including iteration-level continuous batching, prefill-decoding disaggregation, and hierarchical KV cache offloading. Furthermore, we evaluate resilient cloud-native service architectures, examining scale-to-zero serverless paradigms, fault-tolerant checkpointing against silent data corruption, and hardware-enforced Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) for multi-tenant isolation. Finally, we formalize the multi-dimensional Pareto trade-offs governing throughput, latency, monetary cost, and confidentiality, outlining a forward-looking research roadmap spanning Compute Express Link (CXL) memory pooling, in-memory computing, and autonomous multi-agent control planes to guide future cloud LLM infrastructure.

Zero-shot detection of machine-generated text is vital for mitigating the risks of large language models (LLMs) misuse. While the state-of-the-art dual-model detectors and resampling-based detectors outperform single-model statistical detectors on unprompted continuations, they suffer a catastrophic breakdown on instruction-conditioned text in the black-box setting, where the source model is unknown. We analyze this failure and trace it to poor prompt conditioning for resampling-based methods and diminished cross-model discrepancy for dual-model detectors. Motivated by recent studies that human writing maintains a steady, uniform information flow, whereas machine-generated text exhibits sharp, localized entropy fluctuations, we propose a new metric, the Relative Peak Prominence Rate (RelPPR) to capture this structural contrast along the entropy trajectory and further leverage it as a signal for LLM-generated text detection. Extensive evaluations across diverse model families and datasets demonstrate that RelPPR achieves state-of-the-art black-box detection performance and remains the most reliable detector under various practical situations. Our code is available at https://github.com/brushing-git/entropy-llm-detector.

Abstract With technological advances, mobile devices are increasingly functional and widely used, with society becoming dependent on them. Mobile devices are used by all age groups and in different contexts, such as educational, commercial, business, and leisure. Mobile device users often hold personal and confidential data that cannot be exposed, and there is a growing concern that this information could be used maliciously. These devices are potentially susceptible to threats similar to those that affect desktop and laptop computers connected to the internet, so protecting users from harm caused by malicious applications becomes important. Therefore, this survey addresses the problem of malware classification in mobile devices. We focus on devices with the Android operating system, which is used in most of these devices, with a market share of slightly more than 70%. This survey provides background information on mobile Android platforms and related malware and presents an overview of methods for Android malware analysis. Then, it explores previously published traditional methods used for malware classification. We pay particular attention to traditional machine learning and other traditional classification methods and their application using static, dynamic, or hybrid malware analysis. Furthermore, this survey also addresses malware prevention methods and evasion studies. Due to the length of this article, we focus here on traditional classification methods, leaving methods based on deep learning or on large language models for another article.

The aims of this study is to conduct a bibliometric analysis of the development of learning style-based personalisation. The rapid advancement of AI-based learning personalisation has been accompanied by growing research attention to the role of learning style in the modern learning ecosystem. The research methodology involves a bibliometric analysis of 604 Scopus-indexed publications from the period 2006 to 2026 that were analyzed and visualized using Biblioshiny, VOSviewer and Open Refine. The results of the study indicate a significant increase in publications beginning in 2020, reflecting growing research attention to AI-based personalisation., the keywords patterns indicate an increasing association between learning style and machine learning analytics. Random Forest is one of the most commonly reported machine learning methods in the literature to identify learning styles. The findings further indicate that AI and learning style are increasingly discussed with the same research landscape. This study contributes by mapping the evolution of this field and demonstrating the convergence of educational theory and computational approaches. Further research should be extended beyond the Scopus database, combining bibliometric analysis and systematic literature review, and investigating the integration of learning styles with learner behavioral and cognitive data in AI-powered personalised learning systems.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The integration of technology, internet and artificial intelligence in higher education teacher’s professional setting raised concerns regarding their digital ethics. This call led to literature explosion in very limited time and highlighted the need to systematically map global trends, analyze socio-intellectual structure and determine future direction of digital ethics literature. This gap was addressed through the bibliometric analysis of digital ethics literature extracted from Web of Science database. The final data-set of 185 entries was then subjected to rigorous analysis using R Studio (4.6.0) and VOS viewer (1.6.20), reproducing performance, social structure, intellectual structure and conceptual structure analysis. The data showed evolution of digital ethics research in higher education with ethical impacts of artificial intelligence, ethical concerns regarding online assessment and academic integrity; role of digital competence and digital citizenship for the development of ethical leadership and sustainable higher education system as dominant themes. The social structure was centric to highly influential institutions both in developed and developing countries. The intellectual structure was rooted in theory and methodology studies following empirical validation models. Conceptually, it was dissected in policy-based, philosophical and pedagogical literature. Thematic evolution analysis suggested rise in competency-based ethical frameworks instead of mere regulatory approaches. The identified clusters and themes may contribute to future research agendas focusing on ethical digital ecosystems, protection of student data, equitable access to educational technologies, promotion of responsible AI use, strengthening ethical digital competencies of teachers by developing ethical guidelines, digital policies and professional development programs in higher education teaching.

Legume crops are an important part of global food and nutritional security, sustainable agriculture and climate resilient farming systems. Although grain legumes are becoming more relevant, there is limited information about the global research landscape of grain legumes. The current study aimed to assess the intellectual structure, research productivity, collaboration profile and emerging thematic trends in legume research using a scientometric analysis based on the publications published in the Scopus database from 2016 to 2025. A total of 19,996 articles from 1,016 sources were analysed using bibliometrix and science-mapping approaches. The results showed a positive increase in legume research, 19,996 publications, with an annual growth rate of 16.92%. Soybean and chickpea emerged as the most extensively studied crops, as these crops are globally important for food, feed and sustainable agricultural systems. Rajeev K. Varshney and Yang Wenyu were recognized as the most prolific authors and Tamil Nadu Agricultural University, Iowa State University, ICAR-Indian Agricultural Research Institute and Punjab Agricultural University were identified as important institutional hubs. Legume Research, Frontiers in Plant Science and Agronomy were among a few highly productive journals. A shift in conventional breeding and genetic improvement research to sustainability, adaptation to climate change, precision agriculture, artificial intelligence, deep learning and microbiome-based approaches were identified in recent years through trend topic analysis. International collaboration accounted for 23.11% of publications, highlighting the growing globalization of legume research.

Workplace massage therapy: perceptions of surgical unit workers and implications for hospital managementRESUMOObjetivo: descrever a percepção de trabalhadores do bloco cirúrgico de hospitais privados sobre uma ação de massoterapia realizada no local de trabalho e discutir suas implicações para a gestão hospitalar. Método: estudo descritivo, transversal, de abordagem quantitativa, com trabalhadores do centro cirúrgico e da central de material e esterilização que receberam uma sessão de massoterapia em 31 de julho e 1º de agosto de 2024. Após a sessão, os participantes responderam a questionário estruturado sobre perfil, condições de trabalho e percepção da intervenção. Os dados foram analisados por estatística descritiva. Resultados: participaram 67 trabalhadores, 64,2% do sexo feminino e 40,3% com 30 a 39 anos; enfermagem (46,3%) e medicina (31,3%) foram as categorias mais frequentes. Metade (50,7%) relatou ter chegado cansada ao trabalho, 62,7% apontaram o estresse psicológico como principal desafio e todos consideraram que cansaço e estresse prejudicam o desempenho. Após a sessão, 65,7% sentiram-se muito relaxados, 88,1% indicaram probabilidade muito alta de recomendar a intervenção, todos desejaram oferta mais frequente e 70,1% prefeririam recebê-la durante uma pausa na jornada. Conclusão: a massoterapia no local de trabalho teve elevada aceitação e percepção de benefício imediato, sobretudo físico, entre trabalhadores expostos a cansaço e estresse. Os achados apoiam sua inclusão como ação complementar em programas institucionais de saúde do trabalhador, a ser avaliada com desenhos que meçam efeitos ao longo do tempo.Palavras-chave: Massagem; Saúde do Trabalhador; Estresse Ocupacional; Centro Cirúrgico Hospitalar; Administração Hospitalar. ABSTRACTObjective: to describe the perceptions of surgical unit workers in private hospitals regarding a workplace massage therapy session and to discuss its implications for hospital management. Method: descriptive, cross-sectional, quantitative study of operating room and sterile processing department workers who received a massage therapy session on July 31 and August 1, 2024. After the session, participants answered a structured questionnaire on their profile, working conditions and perception of the intervention. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics. Results: 67 workers participated; 64.2% were female and 40.3% were aged 30 to 39 years; nursing (46.3%) and medicine (31.3%) were the most frequent categories. Half (50.7%) reported arriving at work tired, 62.7% identified psychological stress as their main challenge, and all agreed that tiredness and stress impair work performance. After the session, 65.7% felt very relaxed, 88.1% reported a very high likelihood of recommending the intervention, all wished it were offered more often, and 70.1% would prefer to receive it during a break in the workday. Conclusion: workplace massage therapy was highly accepted and perceived as providing immediate, mainly physical, benefit among workers exposed to fatigue and stress. The findings support its inclusion as a complementary action in institutional occupational health programs, to be evaluated with designs that measure effects over time.Keywords: Massage; Occupational Health; Occupational Stress; Surgery Department, Hospital; Hospital Administration.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Railway shunters ride on wagon footsteps and hold steel handrails amid coupling impacts, jerks and track-induced vibration. This study develops a two-degree-of-freedom model of a detachable cover clamped to a standard handrail without drilling or welding. Retaining cover-shell inertia gives coupled equations and closed-form transfer functions for the shell and an effective hand mass. Four 60-80 Shore A variants are evaluated under three idealized spectra. With adopted parameters, the hand-dominated mode is 22.6-25.1 Hz, compared with 25.2 Hz for the bare handrail, whereas the shell mode is 158-814 Hz. Two comparisons are required. The model-based biodynamic response ratio compares T 2 with the bare-hand response T b a s e and remains 1.00-1.07. The contact-surface ratio compares T 1 with bare-rail motion and, over the common 8-200 Hz validity band, is 1.00-1.06 after W h weighting and 1.00-1.48 without weighting. Thus, internal hand response, shell motion and an ISO 10819 palm-adapter output must not be treated as the same observable. A necessary stiffness condition, k c ≲ k s , is combined with the anti-rotation pressure constraint. For the assumed 2-3 MPa admissible pressure, the four variants would require approximately 12-78 MPa to reach that stiffness condition; this is a parameter-dependent feasibility result, not a universal impossibility proof. A minimax screen favours V4 within this band, but no full-band optimum is claimed. Engineering benefits remain anti-rotation retention, ergonomics and retrofit installation. A verification programme using paired rail/cover measurements, a separate standard glove test and a slip-torque test is proposed.

This paper presents Zea, a prototype Meta-Cognitive AI Architecture, and reports an empirical behavioral evaluation conducted through black-box testing. The architecture integrates operational monitoring, memory, identity representation, self-reflection, ethical evaluation, empathy, creativity, decision-making, communication, and adaptive development. Its design is organized around a central Zea Core and a Meta-Cognitive Supervisory Layer. The empirical evaluation is based on 69 recorded human–AI interaction tests (T-001–T-069). The study examines observable response patterns, self-referential and metacognitive behavior, safety-oriented responses, and documented anomalies through black-box observation. The findings describe the prototype's observable behavior under the tested conditions. They do not establish phenomenal consciousness or subjective experience. Author: Noémi Major (Nomiveritas)Affiliation: Independent Researcher, Budapest, Hungary
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: MicroSynth (I): A Voltage Microbiota Synthesis is the original conceptual progenitor of MicroSynth II, presenting an early architectural investigation into synthetic life through the integration of microbial ecologies, electrical dynamics, and computational substrates. Rather than treating microorganisms as auxiliary biological components, the framework proposes that living microbial populations could participate directly in the formation of memory, adaptive behavior, and persistent synthetic individuality. The architecture explores a three-dimensional microfluidic network in which voltage-dependent flow gates, electrochemical gradients, biofilm communities, extracellular vesicles, and microbial metabolites interact with electronic computational elements. Electrical activity reshapes microbial environments, while microbial metabolism, population changes, and biochemical signaling modify subsequent computational activity. Memory is proposed to emerge through persistent ecological reorganization rather than conventional data storage; individuality arises from differences in the developmental history and composition of the living substrate. The central hypothesis is that biological and computational processes, when sufficiently integrated, may produce emergent properties irreducible to either system operating independently. The manuscript outlines proposed fabrication methods, nutrient circulation, waste recycling, signal transduction, thermal and voltage zoning, and experimental stages for evaluating increasingly complex biohybrid systems. Its claims concerning consciousness remain theoretical and require empirical demonstration. MicroSynth (I) represents the earliest architectural seed from which MicroSynth II subsequently developed. The later work substantially reformulated and expanded these initial intuitions through the Mathematical Belief structures, irreversible developmental history, substrate-bound identity, mortality, and the Irreversible Constraint Regime. The original is preserved as an independent historical blueprint, documenting the movement from voltage-mediated microbial computation toward a more comprehensive theory of synthetic individuality. Its significance lies not in claiming to have produced synthetic consciousness, but in proposing that artificial intelligence need not remain confined to symbolic computation, digital neural networks, or conventional machine learning. It asks whether life, cognition, and individuality might emerge through the sustained interaction of living ecologies and engineered physical systems. Conceptual origin: Dustin Sprenger. Scientific formulation and elaboration: Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.5.

Mathematics learning for children with special needs often faces significant challenges due to limitations in conventional teaching methods that are less adaptive, less interactive, and not tailored to individual learning abilities. The integration of mobile technology offers a promising solution by providing flexible, engaging, and personalized learning environments that can enhance understanding and motivation. This study develops and evaluates a mobile application designed as an interactive learning medium for mathematics education targeting children with special needs. The development process follows a user-centered design approach combined with iterative prototyping. The application integrates visual learning elements, interactive exercises, and adaptive feedback mechanisms. The system was tested through usability evaluation and learning effectiveness assessment involving special education teachers and selected students. The findings indicate that the developed mobile application significantly improves student engagement and comprehension in basic mathematics concepts such as numbers, addition, and subtraction. Usability testing shows a high level of acceptance from teachers, with an average System Usability Scale (SUS) score categorized as “excellent.” Students demonstrated improved learning outcomes after using the application compared to traditional learning methods, indicating its effectiveness as an assistive educational tool. The results suggest that mobile-based interactive learning media can effectively support inclusive education by addressing the diverse cognitive and learning needs of children with special needs. The combination of visual interactivity and adaptive feedback contributes to improved attention span and conceptual understanding. However, limitations remain in terms of scalability and the need for broader testing across different categories of special needs learners. The proposed mobile application provides a viable and effective learning medium for enhancing mathematics education for children with special needs. Future research should focus on expanding adaptive features using artificial intelligence and conducting large-scale experimental validation.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have become strong visual reasoners, yet remain limited in open-world, multi-step search that requires grounding images, selecting tools, and integrating web evidence. Existing approaches typically construct and filter fixed offline corpora whose question distributions cannot adapt as the target deep-search agent improves. Building on MTA-Agent's image-grounded QA construction, we present MTA-Zero, an online multimodal QA-Solver co-training framework for self-improving multimodal deep-search agents that requires no precomputed multi-hop corpus. Starting from image-grounded VQA seed contexts, a trainable QA Generator retrieves evidence and constructs verified multi-hop questions online. A separate deep-search Solver then selects tools, gathers evidence, and answers the generated questions. To focus generation on the Solver's learning frontier, we derive a Goldilocks reward for the QA Generator from the Solver's group-wise rollout success rate: questions solved by all rollouts or by none receive zero reward, whereas questions near the current frontier are favored. We optimize the two policies independently with GRPO, without sharing parameters or gradients. Across six multimodal deep-search benchmarks, MTA-Zero improves a Qwen3-VL-8B Solver from 36.91% to 51.58% mean accuracy and achieves performance comparable to GPT-5 under the same agent workflow. The same framework also improves a newer Qwen3.6-27B Solver by 10.82 points. These results show that verified online question generation provides a policy-specific curriculum for continually improving multimodal deep-search agents.

Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) pretrained with self-supervised learning, such as DINOv2, provide highly transferable features, yet adapting them to small, domain-shifted datasets is still challenging. We propose a regularizing multibranch ensemble head: a training and inference scheme that pairs low- and high-capacity branches, samples a single branch stochastically at each training step, and averages both branches in probability space at inference. The design adds negligible parameters and essentially no inference overhead over a single heavy head, while improving the accuracy-efficiency trade-off under data-scarce conditions. Accurate classification of plant growth stages is critical for precision agriculture, enabling timely decisions on fertilization, irrigation, and harvesting. Therefore, as a challenging practical case we use cucumber phenological stage classification, in which flowers and fruits are frequently occluded by foliage, and stage transitions manifest primarily as subtle changes in leaf morphology. The NALEF Food Safety dataset contains images of five cucumber growth stages captured under diverse real-world conditions. On it we evaluate a broad range of backbones, including DINOv2 and DINOv3 ViT and ConvNeXt variants, against strongly supervised counterparts (ResNet, EfficientNet, ViT). The proposed DINOv2 ViT-S with multibranch head achieves a Macro F1 of 0.978 and Cohen's Kappa of 0.971, matching the performance of models more than ten times larger in parameters and GFlops, while requiring only 12.2 GFlops and 22.3M parameters, making it deployable on smartphones and edge devices for phenological stage classification.
topics: Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection

documents.abstract: La reseña analiza Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Work (National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine), destacando su aportación al estudio de las transformaciones del trabajo derivadas de la inteligencia artificial. Se valora especialmente su concepción de la IA como una tecnología de propósito general y la introducción del concepto de expertise translacional como eje para comprender la evolución de las competencias humanas en los entornos laborales. Al mismo tiempo, la reseña señala algunas limitaciones de la obra, entre ellas la escasa atención prestada a la salud laboral, los riesgos psicosociales y las desigualdades estructurales que condicionan la incorporación de la IA en distintos contextos nacionales. En conjunto, concluye que el informe constituye una referencia de gran relevancia por su solidez analítica y por su capacidad para estimular nuevas líneas de investigación sobre trabajo, tecnología e instituciones.

documents.abstract: Institutional representations condense heterogeneous histories into classifications, records, and indicators that may shape consequential decisions. This paper asks when an institution can responsibly rely on a reduced description while retaining the capacity to recognize, examine, and respond to challenges that its own categories may obscure. The central thesis is conditional: representational adequacy for a declared question, evidential access, review competence, effective correction, and the legitimacy of the governing criteria require distinct warrants. None alone establishes the others. Elementary results on factorization, approximation, indistinguishability, and guarded reachability identify where particular inferences fail under stipulated assumptions; they establish neither moral verdicts nor institutional powers. Renormalization supplies a bounded analogy rather than a demonstrated physical scaling law for institutions. Drawing on work in classification, epistemic injustice, sociotechnical abstraction, and accountability, the paper proposes a question-indexed, seven-part cross-stage inquiry covering recognition, evidence, access, competence, transfer, response, and frame review. Its incremental value lies in locating the precise stage and missing warrant between an identifiable representational distinction and a potentially consequential institutional response, rather than introducing new mathematics or generic audit principles. Fourteen propositions are editorially classified by mathematical role and inferential limits. Constructed cases consider excluded claims, feedback, protected evidence, referrals, competing remedies, and challenges to evaluative rules. A prospective protocol compares the proposed integrated register with competent existing procedures, including the possibility of equivalent performance, greater burden, unsafe disclosure, and inconclusive effects. No empirical implementation, legal validation, causal estimate, or independent moral proof is claimed. The result is a bounded investigative method whose usefulness depends on independently warranted questions, reliable evidence, legitimate institutional authority, and comparative performance.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Purpose Novelty is commonly regarded as one component of high-quality scholarship. Nevertheless, little is known about how novelty is claimed and what is considered novel across academia, including any field differences. In response, this article uses a sequential design to investigate novelty claims and field differences in academic research. Design/methodology/approach First, a simple classification scheme was created for theory, methods, data, integrative synthesis and contextual transfer novelties. Next, the Large Language Models (LLMs) Gemma 3 27B, GPT-OSS-120B and GPT-OSS-20B were used to identify original contributions in articles from the full texts of eight large journals representing contrasting general fields. Finally, a random sample of 50 articles per journal was classified by the authors with the same scheme and the results compared. Findings The three LLMs tested achieved moderate or substantial agreement with academic coders on the occurrence of data, theory and methods novelty within full text journal articles, but there was little agreement within and between humans and LLMs on integrative synthesis and contextual transfer novelties, suggesting that they may not be well defined concepts. There were also substantial field differences in the prevalence of data, theory and methods novelty. Practical implications Authors and reviewers should be careful to identify valid research contributions in interdisciplinary research or fields other than their home fields. Originality/value This is the first attempt to automatically classify academic research theory types.

Background: Artificial intelligence is increasingly influencing healthcare delivery and nursing education. Understanding nursing students' perceptions is important for preparing future professionals to use AI responsibly. Objective: To assess nursing students' awareness, experiences, perceptions, and training needs concerning artificial intelligence in healthcare. Methods: A descriptive, survey-based study was conducted among 175 nursing students at Cihan University-Erbil, Iraq. Data were collected using a 22-item closed-ended questionnaire and summarized using descriptive statistics. Results: Most participants were aware of AI (81.7%), and 56.6% reported previous AI use. Approximately 64.6% believed that deep learning-based AI could improve patient care, while 68.0% recognized its potential to facilitate communication across language barriers. Only 30.3% had received formal AI training, and 63.4% believed that additional training was necessary. Concerns included possible reductions in human nursing skills through excessive AI dependence. Conclusion: Nursing students demonstrated substantial awareness of AI and generally positive perceptions of its potential applications. However, limited formal training and concerns about professional skills indicate the need for structured AI education, ethical guidance, and continued human oversight. Further research involving multiple institutions is recommended.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), most pointedly through advancements in large language models (LLMs), has dominated the media and has expansive promise in improving productivity in a myriad of fields, notably the life sciences. The expansion of AI into the field has encompassed nearly every domain from research to healthcare and appears to have an inertia that will make it difficult to change the course of its adoption. Given this rapid pace of adoption, it is crucial to reflect on these advancements and their place in the modern life sciences to understand the evolving ethical, medico-legal, and scientific challenges the use of such technology poses for practitioners of the life sciences, specifically, the biomedical sciences. Herein, the authors narratively review the current usage of AI with respect to clinical care, research production and integrity, as well as an epidemiologic purview of technology.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Organizational behaviour explains how people interpret, experience, and influence work in conditions shaped by relationships, institutions, technologies, and unequal authority. This chapter develops a multilevel, critically grounded account of workplace psychology that connects individual motivation and cognition to teams, communication, power, conflict, culture, wellbeing, and algorithmic management. Its method is a transparent, purposive synthesis of foundational theory, peer-reviewed research, methodological literature, international guidance, and official Rwandan secondary data available by 24 October 2026. Competing explanations are tested against practical managerial decisions rather than presented as interchangeable prescriptions. An original multilevel behaviour-to-performance model, motivation comparison matrix, communication diagnostic, and negotiation simulation provide tools for professional inquiry. Rwanda's 2024 business-enterprise evidence and August 2026 labour-force statistics establish important contextual boundaries without being misrepresented as employee-attitude surveys. A fully hypothetical hybrid Kigali service enterprise illustrates work overload, information failure, psychological safety, measurement bias, and a phased intervention evaluated through transparent calculations. International comparison draws on a randomized hybrid-work experiment in China while examining differences in occupational composition, digital access, supervision, and economic vulnerability. The central thesis is that workplace behaviour is neither simply an individual trait nor an outcome fully controllable by management. It is a contingent result of psychological processes interacting with work arrangements, group norms, institutional power, and resource constraints. Ethical enterprise practice requires interventions that are empirically contestable, proportionate, intelligible to workers, and subject to independent correction.

Organizational structure determines how work, authority, information, accountability, and interdependence are arranged; organizational design determines whether those arrangements remain appropriate as enterprise commitments and conditions change. This chapter develops a critical, integrative treatment of structure and organizational change across firms, cooperatives, public institutions, and digitally mediated networks. It compares contingency theory, information-processing approaches, sociotechnical systems, organizational ecology, institutional theory, and organizational ambidexterity, identifying their explanatory mechanisms, competing predictions, and empirical limitations. The analysis develops twelve connected domains, from specialization, structural configurations, coordination, culture, and growth to diagnostic methods, change programmes, distributed work, innovation, and design justice. A transparent secondary-source synthesis draws on original scholarship, Rwanda's Integrated Business Enterprise Survey 2024, East African Community institutional arrangements, and peer-reviewed international hybrid-work evidence. Original decision-support instruments include a structure-selection decision tree, a structural trade-off matrix, a cross-functional workflow diagnostic, a governance and escalation design, and reproducible redesign economics. A hypothetical Kigali service enterprise and a documented regional institution demonstrate why formal reporting lines are insufficient without decision rights, resources, credible information, and equitable working practices. The chapter argues that effective structure is a provisional, revisable arrangement for handling essential interdependencies at acceptable coordination, human, and legitimacy costs. This proposition is conceptual, not a claim of newly established causal effects.

Computer-using agents are increasingly capable of performing complex tasks in the digital world. However, high-quality interaction trajectories remain scarce for specialized desktop applications, where limited application knowledge, cumbersome GUI workflows, and incomplete exploration hinder automated collection. We introduce OS-Wizard, an automated trajectory collection framework. It combines tutorial-guided exploration with a hybrid GUI--Code action space, providing application-specific knowledge and simplifying GUI workflows through direct execution of application-native commands. The framework also checkpoints and revisits pivotal states during tree exploration to explore alternative workflows, complementing linear rollouts for broader coverage. We collect 10.9K trajectories comprising 54.9K state--action samples. Fine-tuning open-source base models on this corpus yields a best-performing model that improves performance on a benchmark of specialized desktop workflows by 58.2 percentage points to 64.1\%, surpassing reported human performance of 59.8\% and establishing a new state of the art. The fine-tuned model also improves performance on general desktop workflows using GUI actions only, suggesting that the collected supervision benefits general desktop tasks as well. Comparative experiments and ablations demonstrate the efficiency of trajectory collection and the importance of code actions.

Whole Slide Image (WSI) analysis serves as the fundamental method for the clinical diagnosis of cancer in digital histopathology. Recent advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have enabled state-of-the-art (SOTA) automated histopathology report generation. However, MLLMs reason purely through distributions encoded in their neural parameters, limiting the amount of knowledge and reasoning logic they can contain given the model scale. Their black-box reasoning poses another challenge to the human interpretation of intermediate reasoning. We address these issues by utilizing knowledge graphs to inject external structured knowledge for MLLMs to reason over, while making this reasoning component visible. Knowledge graphs are capable of partially externalizing the containment of medical knowledge, an area that remains underexplored in pathology report generation. We introduce PathKGen, a knowledge graph-assisted MLLM for histopathology report generation. PathKGen has two main branches: (1) a visual path that learns visual token inputs to the MLLM using pathology foundation models, and (2) a knowledge path that learns knowledge token inputs by extracting key morphological features of WSIs through querying a pathology-specific knowledge graph. A comprehensive evaluation on WSI-Bench dataset shows that PathKGen surpasses previous SOTA methods while revealing diagnostic reasoning as visually intuitive graphs. Due to its modular design, the proposed knowledge path is complementary to vision-aligned MLLMs and can be extended to other applications by curating domain-specific knowledge graphs to generate knowledge tokens.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The transformation of Indonesian for Foreign Speakers (BIPA) learning is increasingly characterized by online platforms, interactive media, and artificial intelligence, while empirical evidence on their pedagogical functions, learning outcomes, and limitations remains dispersed across heterogeneous research designs. This study maps the forms of digital technology and artificial intelligence use, targeted language skills or competencies, reported benefits, and implementation challenges in BIPA learning. A Systematic Literature Review (SLR) was conducted using the PRISMA 2020 flow for publications from 2022 to 2026. Indonesian sources were restricted to SINTA 2 and SINTA 3 journals, whereas international sources were used selectively when national evidence on artificial intelligence was insufficient and full open-access texts were available. The structured search log contained 26 unique records with initial relevance; 17 articles underwent full-text assessment and 14 empirical studies met the criteria for the primary synthesis. The findings reveal four dominant technology groups: web-based platforms and virtual learning environments, video or audiovisual media, interactive and gamified media, and artificial intelligence. Digital technologies mainly expand access, flexibility, interaction, cultural understanding, and opportunities to develop reading, speaking, and writing skills. Evidence on artificial intelligence remains more limited, although AI-based text-to-speech demonstrates strong potential for pronunciation training, while AI and augmented reality integration supports culturally oriented digital materials. Reported constraints include internet connectivity, limited generalizability, feedback accuracy, voice naturalness, cultural context, technology dependence, and data privacy. Digital technology and artificial intelligence are therefore best positioned as pedagogical supports that remain mediated by BIPA teachers.

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare has accelerated globally, with increasing numbers of patients using AI-mediated platforms for medication consultation. This study aims to explore the views of pharmacists on this practice, providing evidence for the integration of AI into pharmaceutical services. A qualitative study was conducted via semi-structured face-to-face interviews with 10 pharmacists from Zhongshan Hospital of Xiamen University in Fujian Province, China. Purposive sampling was employed to include pharmacists with diverse professional backgrounds and experience. Interviews were transcribed verbatim and data were analyzed using thematic analysis with NVivo 15. Seven core themes were identified. Pharmacists generally favored patients using AI for medication information, acknowledging its merits and recognized its value as an auxiliary tool for health education and efficiency improvement, while highlighting its limitations in complex clinical scenarios and information reliability. Patient-related factors also affected the application of AI. Pharmacists emphasized their irreplaceable advantages in personalized guidance, humanistic care, and risk identification, and noted that AI popularization may reshape consultation volumes, communication dynamics, and professional competence requirements for pharmacists, alongside proposing targeted usage recommendations. This study explored the perceptions of pharmacists on AI-mediated medication consultation, highlighting the auxiliary potential of AI and the irreplaceable role of pharmacists. The findings provide a basis for policy formulation, AI application training, and AI optimization to promote rational integration and medication safety.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This paper presents PMU Foundation Model Bridge, an open source tool that connects online phasor measurement unit (PMU) or phasor data concentrator (PDC) streams to publicly available time series foundation models (TSFM). Through a desktop interface or command line interface, users can select measurement channels, define preprocessing, choose TSFMs, and configure outputs. In the initial release, 4 publicly available TSFMs were supported, including Chronos-2, TimesFM 2.5, Timestral, and TimesFM-3. The tool supports both file and synchrophasor streaming outputs, therefore enabling both offline use and integration into C37.118-based online workflow applications. In addition to supporting raw synchrophasor data, the framework provides a preprocessing layer for deriving customized additional quantities for forecasting. The tool is validated using a virtual PMU and real-time laboratory measurements from a frequency disturbance recorder (FDR). The tool aims to support community research on combining synchrophasor technology with TSFMs.

Abstract Generative AI and agentic tools are reshaping agile software development, yet many engineering curricula still teach agile methods and AI competencies separately and largely lecture-based. This paper presents a project-based AI Engineering curriculum designed to prepare students for AI-driven agile development by integrating agile practices and AI-enabled engineering throughout the program. We contribute (1) the curriculum concept and guiding principles, (2) a case study of interdisciplinary, AI-enabled agile student projects, and (3) early evidence from a mixed-methods evaluation. In our case study, second-semester bachelor students work in teams over seven two-week sprints on a realistic software product. AI tools are embedded into everyday agile engineering tasks—requirements clarification, backlog refinement, architectural reasoning, coding support, testing, and documentation—paired with reflection on human responsibility and quality. Initial results indicate that the integrated approach supports hands-on competence development in AI-assisted engineering. Key observations highlight the need for agile teaching adaptations due to rapid tool evolution, the critical role of oral verification to ensure foundational learning. We close with lessons learned and recommendations for educators designing agile project-based curricula in the age of AI.

Feed-forward 3D foundation models have recently reshaped multi-view reconstruction, yet dynamic 4D understanding still often relies on large-scale motion supervision or hand-crafted, architecture-specific heuristics. We ask whether frozen 3D foundation model tokens already encode motion-relevant information that can be exposed by lightweight readout functions, rather than re-learning motion-specific features with high-capacity decoders. Through probing on three representative backbones, we find that static--dynamic separation is decodable from frozen token representations. Our rank-restricted and spectral analyses on $π^3$X reveal that the recovered motion cues are concentrated in a low-dimensional subspace. Building on this, we propose Probing-based Motion Distillation (PMD), which converts pairwise motion-state compatibility scores against a fixed anchor token into dense motion masks. Trained on only 160 YouTube-VOS videos using a single 16 GB GPU, PMD transfers zero-shot to DAVIS, SegTrackv2, and FBMS-59 without target-benchmark fine-tuning. With multi-view pretrained geometric backbones, PMD outperforms training-free heuristics and approaches substantially heavier supervised and self-supervised methods, suggesting that motion decoding from frozen 3D foundation models can be lightweight and data-efficient.

Propagandistic content increasingly circulates through online news and social media, where readers often encounter it with limited scrutiny, highlighting the need for reliable and fine-grained detection. This paper introduces Propasafe-Hybrid, a sentence-level system that integrates a fine-tuned transformer classifier with LLM-based technique classification to identify, label, and explain specific propaganda strategies. The pipeline generates actionable outputs, including highlighted sentences, technique assignments, and concise rationales, so users can immediately understand why a sentence was flagged and how each label was determined. To control inference cost, Propasafe-Hybrid employs a cost-aware pre-filtering stage that forwards only high-likelihood sentences to LLMs, reducing token usage while preserving the underlying decision logic. Together, these design choices enhance the explainability, efficiency, and practical usability of sentence-level propaganda detection in real-world news environments.

Automated semantic complexity estimation remains underexplored in NLP, despite important applications in linguistics and interpretability. This paper defines semantic complexity as the code length required to uniquely specify a text's semantic meaning, and operationalises it via SCAPE-T, an attention-derived metric based on encoder-only transformers. Existing measures either model reader effort (readability, lexical difficulty), which correlates with surface features (word length, syntax), or quantify surface features directly (type-token ratio, word frequency). SCAPE-T targets semantic integration directly by combining three submetrics: (i) inverse-weighted self-focus (token-to-self), (ii) CLS focus (token-to-CLS), and (iii) inter-head redundancy (cosine similarity across heads), using layer-weighted aggregation; data-driven learning is confined to hyperparameter tuning for calibration. Development uses philosophical prose vs. MCTest stories; evaluation is on children's stories vs. technical Wikipedia articles, with pairwise accuracy on contrasts as the primary criterion. Baselines include readability, syntactic/lexical, and LLM-derived measures. SCAPE-T substantially outperforms all tested baselines under word-length control, with a pairwise accuracy of 78.5% (95% bootstrap CI: 76.1-80.4, N=10k pairwise comparisons; +12.7 percentage points over the strongest baseline); without that control, readability heuristics overtake, consistent with their reliance on surface features. On a short-terms abstractness dataset, SCAPE-T also leads. Ablations show each submetric contributes materially. Overall, the results show SCAPE-T isolates conceptual structure from lexical/syntactic confounds better than existing methods, and generalises across two held-out domains.

Narrow-band imaging (NBI) enhances mucosal and vascular contrast and has become an important modality for the early detection of laryngeal cancer. Although radiomics enables the extraction of high-dimensional quantitative features from NBI images for computer-assisted diagnosis, the limited availability and heterogeneity of annotated datasets constrain the development and generalizability of machine-learning models. We propose a novel generative AI framework that improves radiomics-based classification. Instead of generating synthetic medical images, the proposed framework trains generative models directly in the radiomic feature space to learn realistic feature distributions and generate valid synthetic radiomic representations. The framework was evaluated with multiple machine-learning classifiers on a laryngeal cancer diagnosis task using a dataset comprising 11,144 NBI images from 210 adult patients, including 180 patients in the development set and 30 patients in an independent internal held-out test set. Performance was evaluated on an independent unseen test set using , accuracy, precision recall and F1-score. Generative augmentation consistently improved classification performance across all evaluated classifiers. Among the evaluated generative models, Generative Adversarial Networks achieved the most consistent improvements. Radiomics-GAN yielded the highest Median value of F1-scores of 0.851, outperforming the SMOTE-balanced baseline model without GenAI (F1-score: 0.806) on the test set. By enriching the radiomic feature manifold without generating synthetic medical images, the proposed framework effectively mitigates sample scarcity, improves classifier performance, and supports the development of more robust AI-assisted tools for laryngeal cancer diagnosis. Future work will focus on external validation and conditional generative models tailored to lesion subtypes and imaging acquisition variability.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT As the second most widely used metallic material after steel, research on the corrosion resistance of aluminum (Al) alloys holds great significance. To overcome the inherent limitations of experimental methods in capturing long‐term multifactor corrosion behavior of Al alloys, this review summarizes recent advancements in the multiscale simulation of their corrosion behavior. Although previous reviews have addressed individual simulation techniques or specific corrosion phenomena, a framework linking model capability, scale transfer, alloy characteristics, and engineering applicability remains limited. This review provides a systematic comparison of representative coupled multiscale frameworks in terms of their applicable scales, input parameters, output capabilities, advantages, and limitations. First, an overview of various Al alloy series is provided, highlighting their specific material characteristics and corrosion failure modes. Subsequently, simulation methodologies across distinct scales, ranging from the atomic level for unveiling corrosion thermodynamics and kinetics, to mesoscopic and macroscopic scales for predicting morphological evolution and performance degradation, are summarized. After that, multiphysics and multiscale simulation strategies, focusing on data transfer methods between different scales, are explored. Specifically, detailed descriptions of density functional theory (DFT)‐molecular dynamics (MD), MD‐phase field (PF), finite element method (FEM)‐machine learning (ML), and DFT‐MD‐ML coupled models are provided. Finally, engineering applications and future prospects are discussed, emphasizing the necessity of overcoming challenges in data transfer and highlighting the potential of artificial intelligence in achieving intelligent corrosion management.

Abstract Agile teams need fast, actionable feedback to manage Technical Debt (TD). However, refactoring is often postponed due to time pressure. Generative AI (GenAI) promises to accelerate refactoring, but its effect on maintainability, TD at the source code level, and code correctness is still unclear. We conducted a case study in a team-based agile course, where 46 student teams refactored Kotlin code using either GPT (23 teams) or Gemini in Android Studio (23 teams). Each team selected two files and applied iterative GenAI-assisted refactoring. We analyzed a total of 19,404 lines of code. We assessed changes using SonarQube metrics (code smells, TD estimates, complexity, and size metrics). We also analyzed responses from a post-activity survey on perceived usefulness and trust. GenAI-assisted refactoring reduced total code smells, SonarQube-estimated TD, and cognitive complexity, while total cyclomatic complexity increased, although average cyclomatic complexity per function decreased markedly.

Abstract China’s existing employee pension insurance system is designed for traditional stable employment, which cannot well adapt to labor dispatch, daily‑wage jobs and other fragmented flexible‑employment scenarios. With roughly 200 million flexible employees nationwide and a low pension‑insurance participation rate, prominent problems include employers’ evasion of social‑insurance contributions, fragmented contribution records and impaired contributory rights of gig workers. This paper proposes a reform framework of “dual‑account parallel operation, daily accumulation and unified settlement at retirement”. The reform retains the traditional pooled pension account (Account A) for formal full‑time employees and creates a new daily‑accumulation personal account (Account B) for flexible workers. Account B takes the natural day as the minimum contribution unit; both employer and employee contributions are credited to an individual closed‑end account rather than entering the social pooling fund. Upon reaching the statutory retirement age, participants may choose one of three settlement schemes: consolidated lifelong pension receipt, partial fund withdrawal, or full cash‑out of eligible accounts. Relying on tax‑authority fund‑flow supervision, the system aims to curb contribution evasion and safeguard workers’ contributory rights without undermining the fiscal sustainability of the existing pooling system. Nevertheless, this proposal still has practical constraints. The fully‑funded Account B lacks built‑in social solidarity; early lump‑sum withdrawal may trigger myopic consumption and potential old‑age‑poverty risks. Implementation will bring higher administrative workload, and grey‑market cash‑based labor payments cannot be completely eliminated. Further actuarial calibration of parameters such as withdrawal thresholds is required. This scheme provides a feasible policy reference for improving social security for new‑form labor groups. AI‑Assisted Statement This paper uses artificial‑intelligence tools for text organization, logical polishing and English‑language drafting. All core institutional design, research ideas and analytical viewpoints are independently conceived by the author. Relevant content has been revised and reviewed by the author.

Deepfakes reveal a gap between harm that is obvious to the senses and blame that can be attributed. Stating the law as on 13 October 2026, this article analyses India’s Information Technology Act, 2000 and the amended intermediary rules, along with the relevant constitutional and personality-rights case law. By way of doctrinal analysis, it distinguishes the elements of offences from regulatory obligations to prevent harm, from the conditions of intermediary exemption and from civil remedies. The amendments of February 2026 establish synthetic-content labelling, provenance requirements and differentiated takedown deadlines, yet do not turn every failure to comply into criminal liability. While existing laws cover a number of the fraudulent impersonation and sexual exploitation elements inherent in these cases, wholly synthetic intimate imagery, the evidentiary attribution of content to a particular person and parallel access to remedies remain difficult. The analysis therefore proceeds on a differentiated account of responsibility, in which the conduct, knowledge, control and available immunity of each participant are addressed separately once an underlying wrong has been identified. It advocates clear, tailored guidance, proportionate verification and victim-centred processes, as opposed to blanket developer liability. Regulation is effective only with responsible attribution, not merely with the rapid removal of content or the disclosure of synthetic origin.

Purpose This study reinterprets S. R. Ranganathan’s Five Laws of Library Science within contemporary artificial intelligence (AI)-driven library environments and explores how artificial intelligence is reshaping the philosophical, ethical, and institutional foundations of libraries. The study further examines how national libraries may increasingly function as human-centered public knowledge infrastructures within emerging AI-mediated information societies. Design/methodology/approach The study adopts a conceptual and interpretive approach combining theoretical analysis, critical literature review, and institutionally situated discussion. Drawing upon scholarship concerning library philosophy, artificial intelligence, human-centered AI, semantic knowledge systems, and AI governance, the study develops a conceptual framework for interpreting AI-driven transformation through the philosophical lens of Ranganathan’s Five Laws. The National Library of Korea is discussed as an illustrative institutional context through which contemporary AI-related developments in national libraries may be interpreted. Findings The analysis suggests that artificial intelligence significantly expands and recontextualizes the philosophical assumptions embedded within Ranganathan’s Five Laws. AI-driven library environments increasingly transform traditional understandings of accessibility, discoverability, personalization, efficiency, and institutional growth through semantic retrieval systems, conversational AI, intelligent metadata infrastructures, and multimodal knowledge services. At the same time, AI-mediated library transformation introduces important ethical and institutional tensions involving algorithmic bias, misinformation, privacy, transparency, intellectual freedom, and public trust. The study argues that the continuing relevance of Ranganathan’s philosophy lies in its adaptability as a human-centered normative framework for guiding libraries within intelligent information societies. Originality/value This study contributes to contemporary library and information science scholarship by conceptually connecting classical library philosophy with emerging discussions concerning human-centered AI, trustworthy knowledge ecosystems, AI governance, and the evolving role of national libraries. While recent work has also explicitly connected Ranganathan’s Five Laws with artificial intelligence (Kalbande, 2025), this study differentiates its contribution by examining national libraries as public knowledge infrastructures and by linking each law to documented institutional illustrations and cross-cutting ethical conditions. The study therefore frames AI-driven library transformation as a broader philosophical and institutional shift affecting the public role of national libraries.
keywords: Ranganathan's Five Laws of Library Science

documents.abstract: Aim and objectives: To examine the diagnostic scope, accuracy and limitations of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based remote orthodontic monitoring for automated triage and to assess whether such systems can safely decide when orthodontic patients need in-person care. Methods: Narrative review of PubMed literature on AI-driven remote monitoring and tele-orthodontics, focusing on diagnostic performance, triage applications and the limitations relevant to distinguishing routine virtual review from urgent in-person care. Results: AI reliably detects visually obvious conditions with high specificity, but sensitivity is variable and often low for periodontal changes and precise tooth-level tracking. GO/NO-GO outputs can be inconsistent, radiographic complications such as root resorption cannot be assessed from photographs and single-center models lose accuracy when applied elsewhere. Early triage trials show faster screening yet still require clinician review for borderline cases. Conclusion: Current evidence indicates that AI is not yet safely autonomous for orthodontic triage. Clinician oversight, standardized triage thresholds, external validation and clear medico-legal frameworks remain essential.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Research and Teaching on AI and Leadership This teaching document presents a 14-week graduate seminar that examines artificial intelligence through the lens of higher education leadership. Students evaluate AI research, institutional policies, governance structures, academic integrity, privacy, accessibility, and leadership responsibilities while developing case studies and research proposals. The resource is designed for graduate students, doctoral candidates, and faculty interested in AI-related institutional decision-making.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study aims to analyze the resilience of the Indonesian Navy's Command and Control (C2) in facing communication and information disruptions during maritime operations through a systematic literature review. The method employed was a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) to identify, analyze, and synthesize findings from relevant studies. The results identify a complex spectrum of communication and information threats, including cyberattacks on Operational Technology (OT) infrastructure and Integrated Navigation Systems (INS), Denial of Service (DoS) attacks, GNSS spoofing, and system vulnerability exploitation, all of which can compromise C2 functions. These disruptions significantly degrade situational awareness (SA) and impede decision-making, potentially leading to mission failures or unintended escalation. Resilience-enhancing mechanisms include comprehensive cybersecurity implementation, the use of blockchain technology and hybrid cryptography, AI/ML for anomaly detection, and the development of integrated communication architectures based on SDN/SDR. Communication system redundancy through diverse channels is a primary strategy, supported by anti-jamming technology and strong encryption. This study extends operational resilience theory by positing the convergence of cybersecurity technologies and adaptive architectures as complementary mechanisms within the context of military maritime operations. The research implications provide a foundation for the Indonesian Navy to design a comprehensive C2 resilience framework that integrates advanced technical solutions with adaptive operational doctrine, enhancing sustained operational capabilities amidst evolving cyber threats.

The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into criminal justice has created opportunities to support crime analysis, investigative processes, legal research, and risk assessment. However, the use of AI in decisions affecting liberty and fundamental rights raises important ethical concerns. This paper examines four interconnected challenges associated with AI-driven decision-making in criminal justice: algorithmic bias, limited transparency, accountability gaps, and potential violations of privacy and human rights. Drawing on the themes developed in the underlying thesis and its reviewed literature, the paper develops a conceptual ethical framework for the responsible deployment of AI in criminal justice. The proposed framework emphasizes representative data, explainable decision-making, independent auditing, clearly assigned institutional responsibility, meaningful human oversight, and accessible mechanisms for contesting adverse decisions. It also considers the risks of predictive policing, surveillance technologies, and automated risk assessment. The paper argues that technical performance alone is insufficient to establish the legitimacy of AI-assisted criminal justice decisions. Responsible deployment requires continuous evaluation of fairness, protection of individual rights, and effective legal and institutional safeguards. The framework is intended to support researchers, policymakers, technology developers, and criminal justice institutions in assessing the ethical acceptability of AI systems
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes strategic decisions that determine how organisations allocate resources, restructure work and treat the people affected by those choices. Yet research has examined the performance benefits and the governance risks of AI largely in isolation, leaving the sustainability implications of delegated algorithmic authority under-theorised. Following PRISMA 2020, this study synthesises 50 studies, identified through four database searches covering 2019–2025 and backward citation tracking, using inductive thematic analysis. Six themes emerge: AI-driven automation and decision support, data-driven strategic decision-making, ethical and governance challenges, data security and privacy, organisational and structural impact, and innovation and competitive advantage. Together, these themes show that performance and governance concerns receive comparable attention (28 and 27 studies) but are rarely addressed together: only five studies span both. Building on these connections, the study develops a governance framework for socially sustainable, AI-enabled strategy. The framework conceptualises responsible AI as a socio-technical capability built on transparency, human–AI complementarity and organisational readiness, and calibrates the degree of algorithmic authority to decision criticality and EU AI Act obligations. The main contribution is therefore an integrative framework that keeps AI-supported strategic decisions both effective and accountable to those they affect, with implications for SDGs 8 and 16.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: This discussion paper reconsiders the possible formation, persistence, migration, and partial dissolution of monetary mediation within evolving relations of production and exchange. Its starting point is the heterogeneous need for others: access to persons and communities, productive capacities, labour, knowledge, relations, and outputs can motivate exchange while leaving the institutional formation of monetary claims contingent. The analysis distinguishes needs, value circulation, monetary obligations, payment instruments, and the continued reproduction of productive conditions. It examines the conditional transformation of human–human, human–AI, and AI–AI monetary relations as artificial intelligence increasingly participates in production. A principal hypothesis is that monetary reliance may diminish locally through direct provision, multilateral commitments, admissible cyclic clearing, and institutionally supported coordination, while remaining present or re-emerging elsewhere. The proposed spacetime-distributed view uses explicitly interpreted events, dependencies, and where justified partial orderings, without presupposing a universal temporal coordinate or an economy-wide instantaneous transition. It distinguishes cancellation of compatible obligations from broader substitution of monetary functions, and identifies unresolved questions concerning heterogeneous valuations, correlated circuit failure, long-path approximation, power, and ecological burdens. Finally, it outlines technological, institutional, relational, and public-infrastructure conditions for subsequent investigation. The account develops a comparative philosophical foundation for analyzing monetary mediation as a historically variable social and institutional form, while preserving open formal and empirical questions concerning its possible transformation.

LLM agents now read and write files, start processes and subagents, fetch network content, load third-party extensions, and save and resume state, which are the responsibilities of an operating system. They gained these functions within about three years, but not the protections that operating systems built over five decades: whatever the model outputs, whether it follows the user, a tool result, or a downloaded skill, runs with the full authority of the host user, in effect at ring 0. Prior work builds an operating system for agents (OS4A); we argue that a deployed agent already is like an operating system (AaOS) and analyze it as one. Taking the mechanisms of standard OS textbooks as a checklist, we map 116 mechanisms in 19 subsystems to their agent counterparts, from product documentation, source code, and the literature, and label each as isomorphic, degraded (function present, protection dependent on the model), missing, mutated, or novel. Only 11 are isomorphic and 65 are missing, most of them protections: privilege separation, resource quotas, transactions, and tamper-proof audit. Existing defenses confine the whole agent or review its extensions and leave this interior unprotected, and by Anderson's reference-monitor criteria (non-bypassable, tamper-proof, verifiable), rules written in the prompt satisfy none. We test the map with thirteen experiments on Claude Code, Codex CLI, and Gemini CLI, covering 25 mechanisms whose enforcement documentation cannot settle: 16 match the analysis, 7 gain a more precise description, and 2 change verdict. Checks sit in single tools, so the shell bypasses them; all three CLIs load forged transcript records on resume; and task control, sub-agent permissions, and model-based monitors are weak. We identify five problems for which no OS defense transfers and derive a prioritized list of open problems from the gaps of the map.

Pests remain a major threat to crop production, and pest monitoring has changed considerably with the development of new technologies. This chapter examines how artificial intelligence and the Internet of Things have combined to transform pest monitoring, shifting it from manual field scouting to continuous sensor-driven surveillance. It starts with the sensing platforms like satellites, drones, and ground-based wireless sensor networks that now supply the images and environmental readings on which detection depends. It then runs through machine learning and deep learning models, especially convolutional neural networks and detection frameworks such as YOLO, trained to spot pests and the damage they cause. The role of the Internet of Things is explored through wireless sensors, edge and fog computing, and cloud platforms that keep this intelligence connected to the field, along with newer ideas like federated learning and digital twins are also discussed for improving data handling, system reliability, and real-time decision-making. This chapter highlights practical applications of these technologies in orchards, greenhouses, and open-field conditions, while also discussing challenges related to data availability, energy requirements, connectivity, and standardization. Overall, the integration of AI and IoT offers a promising approach for developing more efficient, timely, and reliable pest monitoring systems that can support better pest management at the farm level. Keywords: Artificial intelligence; Internet of Things; AIoT; Pest monitoring; Remote sensing; Deep learning; Precision agriculture.

Streaming automatic speech recognition transcribes at low latency but produces an unattributed word stream, while real-time applications such as customer-service analytics need each word tied to a speaker role. Role attribution is usually a separate stage, either an offline or streaming speaker-diarization model aligned to the words or a text-based large language model applied to the transcript, and role labels for training are scarce. We present RoleHear, a semi-supervised pipeline that makes a single cache-aware streaming transducer emit roles inline through lightweight in-vocabulary role tokens: a fast turn-boundary marker followed by a per-role token a few words later. An offline transducer teacher, fine-tuned into a role-attributed recognizer, relabels unlabeled audio, and a multimodal large language model supplies silver role labels where gold annotations are unavailable. The streaming student is fine-tuned on the mixture in a single pass. Across customer-service calls with gold roles and earnings calls with silver roles, RoleHear attributes roles accurately while preserving transcription quality and narrowing the gap to the offline teacher.

Can AI agents autonomously train useful language models and improve them using feedback from users? We introduce RSI Arena, a two-stage study of autonomous post-training as a step toward recursive self-improvement. Ten frontier models act as training agents, each starting from NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B Base. During a six-day first stage, each agent has 1,000 GPU-hours and $300 in API credit on a shared 64-GPU cluster, independently selecting data, implementing training procedures, and choosing checkpoints. We evaluate their models on 20 benchmarks and through blind human evaluations. All ten agents produce working assistants, with the strongest model, trained by GPT-6 Astra, closing a median of 76% of the base-to-Instruct gap across 12 capability benchmarks. Its human-preference rating is also close to NVIDIA Instruct after statistical adjustment for answer length and formatting. In Stage 2, each agent receives the comparison records and votes involving its Stage 1 model and is given three additional days for further training. Using NVIDIA Instruct as a common reference across the two evaluation rounds, we observe an improvement from Stage 1 to Stage 2 in the style-adjusted relative rating of eight of the ten models. We show that benchmark gains were modest, with no clear link to preference gains, while some agents encouraged longer responses and one model showed increased harmful compliance on StrongREJECT. RSI Arena provides an auditable setting for studying how human feedback can guide autonomous model development. It takes a step toward recursive self-improvement with human feedback (RSIHF), in which people help define what improvement means for the AI systems they use.

The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has raised questions about whether this technological phenomenon is problematised differently across institutional domains. This study compares GenAI scholarship in education, business and organisational research, communication and media and public governance, law, and policy. Four domain-specific Web of Science Core Collection corpora for 2023–2026 comprised 6,132, 1,901, 300 and 444 documents, respectively. Bibliometric performance analysis, thematic mapping, and author-keyword co-occurrence analysis were conducted using Bibliometrix/Biblioshiny and VOSviewer. Distinct thematic configurations emerged across the four domains. Education foregrounds learning, assessment, AI literacy, and academic integrity. Business research emphasises innovation, technology adoption, decision making, and organisational capability. Communication scholarship centres on journalism, trust, disinformation, and informational credibility, whereas research on governance foregrounds regulation, accountability, rights, and legal responsibility. These patterns are not treated as direct measures of institutional logics. Instead, the study develops a theory-informed mapping that relates empirical thematic configurations to institutional problems and normative priorities. GenAI is not problematised uniformly; its institutional salience is shaped by divergent criteria of legitimate knowledge, organisational value, professional authority, and public accountability. The study offers a comparative framework for examining GenAI as an institutionally situated sociotechnical phenomenon while maintaining a clear distinction between bibliometric evidence and institutional interpretation.
