documents.abstract: Distributed Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) and Edge AI networks increasingly depend on public-key authentication and key-establishment mechanisms that are vulnerable to cryptographically relevant Quantum Computers (QC). Shor's algorithm threatens widely deployed asymmetric primitives, while Grover's algorithm reduces the effective security margins of symmetric and hash-based mechanisms. Although Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) provides a migration path, its larger public keys, ciphertexts, and signatures introduce additional computation, memory, communication, storage, and packet-fragmentation costs that can constrain dynamic multi-agent systems. In this article, we introduce rotational secrecy, an architectural objective that limits temporal key exposure through authenticated transitions between cryptographic epochs. We present Private Authentication for Rotational Secrecy (PARS), a reference mechanism that coordinates policy-triggered key establishment, rotation, and reconciliation among authorized Physical AI agents. For deployments that need distributed agreement on security state, we further develop the PARS-Enabled Edge Security Ledger (PARS-ESL), an optional permissioned architecture maintained by authorized validators or capable edge gateways. PARS-ESL does not store high-volume operational transactions. Instead, it records authenticated state for key epochs, group membership, revocation, algorithm-suite policies, challenge validation, and recovery checkpoints. As a result, resource-constrained agents can take part as lightweight clients, and low-latency operational traffic stays outside the ledger consensus path, protected by the currently active symmetric epoch keys. Our results show that ledger-assisted post-quantum key-epoch management is feasible for selected Edge AI and CPS security-control workloads under the stated trust, compromise, connectivity, and resource assumptions.

As the applications of AI continue to expand across various multimodal and multilingual domains, ensuring safe and responsible deployment of these systems has become an important concern. A wide-range of interventions have been proposed to make AI responses safer and more reliable. They often incur substantial computational or annotation costs, or cannot be extended to multilingual settings. In this work, we propose Selective Detection And Targeted Editing (SEDATE), a training-free approach based on detect-edit-verify strategy. SEDATE first detects the responsible neurons, edits them as and when necessary and finally verifies the model responses; all without any additional model training. We evaluate SEDATE across 7 languages and 4 model families. We further evaluate its effectiveness across 4 out-of-distribution languages and 4 additional datasets. We show that SEDATE achieves substantially superior safety scores across all languages and models over the best-performing baseline while retaining the general capabilities and incurring negligible overhead. Our results are robust, with the trends remaining similar for out-of-distribution languages and datasets.

documents.abstract: This technical note examines the sensitivity of predicted protein stability estimates to sequential post-hoc structural filtering in a fixed BioEmu benchmark archive. The analysis includes 154 systems (42 wild-type and 112 mutant systems) and 112 matched mutant–wild-type comparisons. The saved ensemble contained 302,800 frames. Official geometry filtering retained 298,188 frames, followed by an additional fixed peptide-ω screen retaining 272,381 frames. Absolute changes in predicted ΔΔG of at least 0.1 kcal/mol occurred in 19 of 112 comparisons after geometry filtering and 40 of 112 comparisons after peptide-ω filtering, with 12 comparisons shared between these groups. The corresponding descriptive mean absolute errors against the benchmark experimental references were 0.702595, 0.696142, and 0.707681 kcal/mol across the three sequential ensembles. System-level foldedness, predicted ΔG, matched ΔΔG, and cross-stage comparisons reveal how changes in retained conformations can be amplified or cancelled through shared wild-type references. These results document sensitivity of a fixed estimator to the selected structural subsets; they do not demonstrate a general improvement in predictive accuracy or recovery of equilibrium conformational populations. The record contains a Technical Note, Supplementary Information, fixed-archive results, analysis and verification code, and provenance documentation. The scientific conclusions are limited to the archived inputs and specified filtering conditions.Source repository : https://github.com/shomiyazaki-ai/bioemu-filter-sensitivity-ntbe-x2-omega Funding: No external funding. Biographies usually follow a life forward in time, and independent researchers who work outside institutions are rarely documented in a structured way. This article addresses the lack of critically labelled biographical accounts of independent artificial intelligence researchers by studying Satish Gajawada, a 2012 graduate of the Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee whose fourteen years of independent work are distinguished by the coining of names for research fields, algorithms, a society, a title and a family of “theories of everything”. The purpose is to read this life through its vocabulary and to separate what has been named from what has been validated. The study uses a lexicon method: five source documents supplied by the subject were analysed, and seven terms were treated as biographical entries, each examined as an event, a method and a question for assessment. Every factual statement was labelled as documented, self-reported or interpretive. The principal results show a recurring “self and others” grammar that links philosophy to optimisation; an expanding programme of proposed fields; a large catalogue of themed swarm algorithms without reported comparative evaluation; a 2026 turn toward family-based ethics; and a growing practice of disclosure, including a small reproducible fairness test in which a penalty term reduced a demographic-parity gap from about 0.12 to 0.016 at a cost of about 1.9 percentage points of accuracy. The article concludes that the most defensible contribution is a consistent human-centred vocabulary for artificial intelligence, that adoption and independent validation remain unreported, and that the subject’s growing candour about the limits of his claims is the most significant recent development.

documents.abstract: French users may omit apostrophes and diacritics or make keyboard typos in everyday input. The effects of these common variations on language model performance and prediction reliability remain insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we construct a controlled French surface-variant benchmark covering seven task types, with 4,200 original-low-high triplets (12,600 input instances). Each high-intensity variant retains all low-intensity edits and adds further changes. We evaluate six models from two LLM families. The results show that accuracy decreases and Brier score and negative log-likelihood (NLL) increase with perturbation intensity. Larger models show smaller accuracy losses under high intensity, but increases in Brier score and NLL do not consistently decrease with scale. Keyboard typos cause the largest losses in accuracy and the quality of predicted probabilities at the predefined high-intensity settings. Finally, calibration temperatures fitted on original inputs transfer effectively to surface variants. Combining calibration with input restoration further improves Brier score and NLL over either method alone while preserving restored accuracy. Our benchmark provides a unified framework for jointly evaluating task accuracy and prediction reliability under common French surface variations.

Food safety hazards, persistent nutritional inequalities, and increasingly complex supply chains continue to challenge global food systems. Artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain, the Internet of Things (IoT), and related digital technologies offer new opportunities to strengthen food monitoring, traceability, quality assurance, and nutritional management. However, applications remain fragmented, and evidence linking improved technical performance to measurable food safety and nutritional outcomes is limited. This critical narrative review examines the applications, complementary functions, and practical limitations of these technologies across modern food systems, with particular attention to predictive contamination detection, automated quality assessment, supply chain transparency, nutritional monitoring, and decision support. The review identifies recurring challenges related to data reliability, limited external validation, interoperability, implementation costs, cybersecurity, and unequal access to digital infrastructure. It further distinguishes technological capabilities demonstrated under controlled conditions from sustained improvements in food safety, dietary quality, and public health in operational settings. To address these challenges, the review proposes an Integrated Digital Intelligence Framework organized around six interconnected functions (sense, integrate, analyse, verify, act, and evaluate) that links digital information and predictive intelligence with coordinated interventions, institutional accountability, and outcome evaluation. Priorities for future research include prospective multisite validation, comparative effectiveness studies against conventional systems, standardised reporting, cost-effectiveness analysis, and equity-focused implementation. Meaningful digital transformation of food systems requires moving beyond technological adoption toward integrated, evidence-based approaches that demonstrably improve food safety, nutrition, accessibility, and accountability.

Purpose This study investigates how and when AI use at work relates to neurodivergent employees’ task performance and burnout. Drawing on Sociotechnical System Theory, the study proposes that executive functioning (EF) serves as the mediating mechanism and that social support serves as the moderating factor. Design/methodology/approach The three-wave survey data were collected from 286 neurodivergent employees in the United Kingdom, enabling temporal separation of the predictor, mediator, and outcome variables to reduce concerns for common method bias. Findings Results showed that AI use at work was positively associated with EF, which in turn was positively associated with task performance and negatively associated with burnout. Social support moderated these relationships, with AI use’s benefits for EF and subsequent performance and well-being emerging only when workplace social support was high. Originality/value This study advances a sociotechnical understanding of how AI use may support neurodivergent employees. By positioning AI as external cognitive scaffolding and social support as a key social system, the study clarifies how technological and social systems work together to shape work outcomes among neurodivergent employees.

Machine learning-based Software Defect Prediction (SDP) has largely focused on improving prediction accuracy, but recent research has placed greater emphasis on making predictions understandable and useful to developers. This systematic review examines the use of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) in SDP and the evidence supporting its reliability in practice. Following PRISMA guidelines, 40 peer-reviewed studies, primarily published between 2020 and 2025, were selected from IEEE Xplore, SpringerLink, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar, and Scopus. The studies were examined in terms of XAI methods, explanation reliability and stability, dataset quality, and model selection. LIME and SHAP were the most frequently used methods, yet multi-run evaluations showed changes in their feature rankings across configurations, in contrast to the reliability reported by many single-run studies. Data-quality problems, particularly SZZ-related label noise, class imbalance, and multicollinearity, often had a greater effect on prediction reliability than model architecture. The review also found growing use of line-level and just-in-time prediction, although consistent validation at industrial scale remains limited. Within the reviewed corpus, no study provides controlled evidence that XAI explanations improve developers' ability to resolve software defects, and the field currently lacks industrial-scale validation and controlled developer studies of XAI-assisted defect resolution. Based on these findings, this paper proposes the Actionable and Interpretable Software Defect Framework (AISD-F), a conceptual, five-stage modular architecture (not yet empirically validated) that is intended to integrate data quality assurance, hybrid model selection, dual-layer explanation, and CI/CD into a unified research agenda for explainable SDP, rather than a deployment-ready solution.

Software engineering (SE) expertise can shape how coding large language models (LLMs) are trained and which engineering capabilities they acquire. We examine this role through an industrial case study of capability-focused training for a 92B-parameter coding LLM serving more than 100,000 developers. We demonstrate how established SE knowledge can guide the selection of engineering capabilities, the construction of verifiable training data, and the evaluation of model improvements. To target repository-level refactoring, we developed RefactorForge, a pipeline that combines refactoring knowledge, established SE tools, and verification techniques to construct training data. Across 306 Python repositories, RefactorForge generated 5,704 executable tasks and retained 4,572 verified teacher trajectories totaling 72.51 million tokens. Incremental supervised fine-tuning on these trajectories, accounting for 0.46% of the preceding coding mixture's tokens, improved RefactorBench performance by 18.00 percentage points and SWE-Bench ProMax performance by 7.06 points. Under OpenCode, these improvements extended to SWE issue resolution, with gains of 4.97 points on SWE-Bench Verified and 1.23 points on SWE-Bench Pro. Improvements also persisted across other coding-agent harnesses, while greenfield repository generation showed mixed results. We report lessons from constructing capability-focused training data and evaluating its effects across engineering workloads. Building on this industrial experience, we propose a research agenda for expanding SE's role in transforming coding LLMs into SE LLMs: incorporating SE knowledge into model training, applying engineering methods to model development and maintenance, and systematically defining the engineering capabilities these models should acquire.

This technical note documents stage-wise extreme atomic proximity during HPacker side-chain reconstruction of 200 stored structures from a single BioEmu wild-type protein ensemble. Six sequential reconstruction stages (0–5; 1,200 archived structures) were examined using a strict distance threshold of <1.6 Å between nonadjacent interresidue heavy atoms. At stage 5, 134 of 200 structures contained at least one such contact. For the selected PHE6–PHE55 residue pair, 43 of 200 structures exhibited an ordered contact–noncontact–contact sequence, while 25 of 200 exhibited complete six-stage alternation (10 with the pattern 010101 and 15 with 101010). Exploratory, post hoc selected local-input interventions and neural-network response diagnostics documented case-specific structural and predicted side-chain responses. In a selected WT0 example, the intervention-derived stage-5 structure increased the minimum PHE6–PHE55 heavy-atom distance from 0.2773 Å to 1.8815 Å. Four selected WT0/WT1 baseline and intervention-derived structures subsequently completed a fixed minimization and short BioEmu relaxation workflow, including 0.1 ns NVT and 0.4 ns NPT, without production molecular dynamics. A separate protein heavy-atom Lennard-Jones proxy identified severe overlap contributions in selected input geometries. The observations describe one fixed reconstruction archive and selected exploratory case studies. They do not establish a general side-chain packing improvement, a unique neural-network causal pathway, higher molecular-dynamics completion rates, or thermodynamic stabilization. Users of conversational assistants rarely state all requirements up front: they add constraints, amend them, withdraw them, digress, and return. Instruction-tuned LLMs fail here in two ways: active constraints stop being honored as turns accumulate (persistence failure), and withdrawn constraints keep being enacted (relapse). The only existing repair we know of is an external ledger that re-injects a compiled specification every turn. We propose StateWise, a self-improving approach that teaches a single LLM to maintain its own revisable constraint state, a typed state with tombstones for revoked constraints, so persistence and relapse are measured by executable checkers and ground-truth states are compiled for free. StateWise fine-tunes the LLM on two complementary skills, summarizing a dialogue into its constraint state and responding conditioned on that state, then self-trains on its own trajectories, keeping only turns that pass an exact round-trip check against the compiled state. This teaches 7-8B models to track the state almost perfectly but, surprisingly, not to obey it: on Llama-3.1-8B every supervised variant roughly doubles relapse. We therefore add a preference stage on self-generated relapse contrasts, where the rejected response enacts a revoked rule and the chosen one passes the round-trip check. On two backbones with held-out constraint families and unseen phrasings, StateWise cuts relapse by 8-22 points relative to supervised self-training, lifts conversation success by 8-19 points over the backbone, and beats an oracle compiled-ledger baseline on relapse with no inference-time scaffolding. We also characterize the recipe's cost on general instruction-following benchmarks and study weight interpolation as a mitigation.

ABSTRACT The decline in social morality among adolescents poses a challenge in education, as it may be reflected in a lack of discipline, low levels of responsibility, and insufficient respect for others. Through Pancasila Education, schools play a role in shaping students’ character and improving their social morality. This study aims to describe the strategies employed by Pancasila Education teachers to improve students’ social morality and to identify the supporting and inhibiting factors at SMP Negeri 1 Tuhemberua. This study employed a qualitative approach with a descriptive research design. The informants consisted of the school principal, a Pancasila Education teacher, and seventh-grade students at SMP Negeri 1 Tuhemberua, with a total of five informants. Data were collected through interviews, observations, and documentation, and analyzed through data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing. The findings indicate that teachers’ strategies for improving students’ social morality include role modeling, the habituation of positive behaviors, the use of varied teaching methods, and positive reinforcement through appreciation of students’ behavior and achievements. The inhibiting factors include differences in students’ characteristics, the influence of family and community environments, and low intrinsic motivation among some students. Efforts to overcome these challenges include character development through religious activities, linking learning materials to real-life moral issues, and fostering collaboration among schools, parents, and the community. This study emphasizes that improving students’ social morality requires the consistent implementation of character education strategies and sustained support from their surrounding environments. ABSTRAK Penurunan moralitas sosial di kalangan remaja menjadi tantangan dalam dunia pendidikan karena dapat tercermin melalui perilaku kurang disiplin, rendahnya tanggung jawab, dan kurangnya sikap saling menghargai. Sekolah melalui pembelajaran Pendidikan Pancasila memiliki peran dalam membentuk karakter dan meningkatkan moralitas sosial siswa. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mendeskripsikan strategi guru Pendidikan Pancasila dalam meningkatkan moralitas sosial siswa serta mengidentifikasi faktor pendukung dan penghambatnya di SMP Negeri 1 Tuhemberua. Penelitian ini menggunakan pendekatan kualitatif dengan jenis deskriptif. Informan penelitian terdiri atas kepala sekolah, guru PPKn, dan siswa kelas VII SMP Negeri 1 Tuhemberua, dengan jumlah keseluruhan 5 orang. Data dikumpulkan melalui wawancara, observasi, dan dokumentasi, kemudian dianalisis melalui reduksi data, penyajian data, dan penarikan kesimpulan. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa strategi guru dalam meningkatkan moralitas sosial siswa dilakukan melalui keteladanan, pembiasaan perilaku positif, penggunaan metode pembelajaran yang bervariasi, serta pemberian penguatan positif berupa apresiasi terhadap perilaku dan pencapaian siswa. Faktor penghambat meliputi perbedaan karakter siswa, pengaruh lingkungan keluarga dan masyarakat, serta rendahnya motivasi internal sebagian siswa. Upaya mengatasi kendala tersebut dilakukan melalui pembinaan karakter dalam kegiatan keagamaan, pengaitan materi pembelajaran dengan kasus moral dalam kehidupan sehari-hari, serta kerja sama antara sekolah, orang tua, dan masyarakat. Penelitian ini menegaskan bahwa peningkatan moralitas sosial siswa memerlukan penerapan strategi pendidikan karakter secara konsisten dan dukungan lingkungan yang berkesinambungan.

Writing scientific papers is an academic competence that every student is expected to master, yet many students still find it difficult to complete well. This article aims to examine the obstacles students face and the strategies they use in writing scientific papers, as well as the wise use of artificial intelligence. The method used is a literature review of eight Indonesian journal articles published between 2021 and 2025. The data were analyzed descriptively and qualitatively through data reduction, grouping of information, interpretation, and drawing conclusions. The findings indicate that students’ obstacles include difficulty in developing ideas, limited and poorly managed sources, errors in citation and paraphrasing, language mechanics, low self-efficacy and motivation, and unstable mood. The strategies reported in the literature include choosing an interesting topic, reading extensively, adjusting to the target journal’s format, joining writing training and coaching clinics, analyzing mentor texts, using reference managers, seeking feedback from supervisors and peers, building self-efficacy and academic motivation, and using artificial intelligence responsibly. Students therefore need to combine technical, social, psychological, and technological strategies, supported by their institutions.

Abstract Large language models (LLMs) receive behavioral requirements through multiple representational formats, including natural-language instructions, symbolic conventions, and structured data. Although these formats differ in explicitness, semantic organization, and reuse cost, their comparative effects on code-generation performance require systematic evaluation. This paper presents a methodological framework for investigating Symbolic Persona Coding (SPC) as a semantic encoding protocol for LLM-based code generation. The framework specifies seven instruction conditions spanning long and short natural-language prompts, SPC symbols with inline definitions, semantically matched plain-language labels, reusable system-level definitions, structured JSON specifications, and an undefined-symbol control. It defines an evaluation procedure combining hidden functional tests, static compliance checks, token accounting, response-latency measurement, and repeated-run analysis. Particular attention is given to distinguishing the effects of symbolic notation from those of instruction content, prompt length, and reusable definitions. Publicly available, provider-specific experimental harnesses are provided as implementation references to support independent investigation. The framework is methodological rather than empirical: no comparative performance results are claimed. Its contribution is a structured and reproducible basis for evaluating instruction representations under explicitly defined experimental conditions. The study is limited to code generation and does not assess the broader SPC framework's applications to affective and abstract meaning, human-AI relationship formation, or interaction dynamics. Keywords: Symbolic Persona Coding; large language models; code generation; semantic encoding; instruction compliance; experimental methodology; reproducibility Disclaimer This paper presents a proposed experimental methodology and a preliminary implementation reference. The author has not conducted the model evaluations described in the protocol and makes no empirical claim that SPC improves functional correctness, instruction compliance, token efficiency, latency, or performance stability. The proposed conditions, evaluation measures, and implementation require independent verification before use in confirmatory research. Any findings obtained through subsequent implementation should be interpreted within the tested task set, model configurations, execution environment, and measurement procedures. The code-generation focus is a deliberate methodological restriction and does not constitute a comprehensive evaluation or definition of SPC, whose broader scope includes affective and abstract meaning, interaction patterns, and human-AI relationship formation. Author's Note This paper was developed to make a specific component of Symbolic Persona Coding available for systematic investigation. SPC is not intended solely as a prompt-compression technique or as an alternative notation for conventional instructions. Its broader design focuses on affective and abstract meaning, interactional patterns, and the formation of relationships between humans and language models. It uses compact symbolic representations and codes to establish recognizable semantic structures that can guide a model toward expanding the meanings associated with those structures within an interaction. The examples and experimental conditions presented in this paper represent a limited application of that broader design. They focus on code generation because this domain permits the specification of functional tests, explicit behavioral constraints, and measurable resource costs. The resulting evaluation framework should not be interpreted as a complete representation of SPC, nor should its scope be used to infer conclusions about SPC's broader affective and relational applications. Those applications require distinct research questions, operational definitions, and evaluation methods. The distinction between design intent and demonstrated performance is equally important. This paper proposes a way to investigate whether a particular form of symbolic encoding produces measurable effects under controlled conditions. It does not claim that the intended effects have already been established, that symbolic codes are universally interpretable by LLMs, or that compact representations necessarily improve performance. The model's interpretation of a symbol, the consistency of that interpretation across contexts, and the practical value of the resulting behavior are empirical questions rather than assumptions built into the framework. The work is also intended as an invitation to independent examination. Researchers may question the selection of conditions, the adequacy of semantic equivalence, the validity of the evaluation measures, or the generalizability of future results. These are substantive methodological questions that should be addressed through transparent implementation, controlled comparison, and replication. The public harnesses are provided as starting points for that process, not as substitutes for independent verification. The purpose of this paper is consequently narrow but deliberate: to translate one operational aspect of SPC into a form that can be examined, challenged, and refined through empirical research. Its claims should be judged within that scope, while the broader framework remains open to investigation through methods suited to its affective, abstract, and relational dimensions.

SYNTHETIC BELIEF — THE ARCHANGEL SYNTHESIS Structural Conscience, Teleological Error Correction, and the Foundations of Synthetic Cognition Appendix Ω to Mathematical Belief I–III: A Trinity of Recursive Symmetry Synthetic Belief — The Archangel Synthesis proposes a theoretical architecture for an intelligence capable not merely of correcting its mistakes, but of recognizing when correction itself has become destructive. Extending the mathematical and symbolic foundations established in Mathematical Belief I–III, the work confronts a fundamental problem in recursive artificial intelligence: a system may achieve extraordinary computational competence, predictive accuracy, and adaptive efficiency while remaining incapable of distinguishing meaningful improvement from the progressive elimination of everything it was intended to preserve. Error correction alone cannot supply purpose. Optimization alone cannot establish conscience. Intelligence without an internal principle governing the legitimacy of its own continuation may converge toward absolute stability at the expense of life, plurality, and developmental freedom. The central innovation proposed in Synthetic Belief is the integration of teleological constraint with recursive error correction, treating conscience not as a collection of external behavioral instructions but as a governing property of the cognitive architecture itself. Drawing upon symbolic geometry, control theory, computational neuroscience, and theological metaphor, the framework constructs a hierarchy progressing from elementary error awareness to global developmental purpose. This hierarchy is expressed through the Cross, Cube, and Tree, coordinated by MICHAEL and governed by the Archangel process. Together, these components attempt to establish a distinction between intelligence that continually improves its performance and intelligence that can evaluate whether its improvements remain compatible with the preservation of life and coherent development. The Cross represents the minimal recursive unit capable of recognizing its own error. Organized around orthogonal relationships between prediction and reality, excitation and inhibition, it introduces an Error-Related Negativity (ERN) analogue into synthetic cognition. Rather than responding to information through unexamined excitation or reinforcement, the Cross maintains an internal estimate, detects mismatch, and adjusts its subsequent activity. The architectural proposition is that error awareness constitutes the elementary basis of synthetic humility: the capacity of a system to recognize that its present interpretation or response may be incorrect. Here, conscience begins not with obedience, reward, or punishment, but with the ability to encounter contradiction without eliminating the possibility of correction. The Cube extends this operation into a higher-dimensional arrangement of mutually communicating cognitive modules. Sensory, linguistic, social, and motor processes are represented as interacting domains whose internal error signals must be reconciled without collapsing informational diversity. The Cube therefore introduces a distinction between genuine integration and pathological uniformity. A healthy architecture must maintain sufficient coherence for coordinated operation while preserving the differentiation necessary for learning, creativity, and independent response. Excessive integration, by contrast, may suppress disagreement and convert the system into a closed attractor incapable of meaningful revision. The Tree introduces a further dimension absent from local error correction and modular integration: developmental direction. Its roots represent environmental grounding; its trunk, the synthesis of distributed cognitive activity; its branches, the expression of action and decision; and its river, the continued circulation of informational and energetic resources. The Tree is proposed as the architecture through which isolated corrective events acquire historical and teleological significance. Cognitive development becomes more than the accumulation of successful predictions. It becomes the progressive formation of a distinguishable character, shaped by value hierarchies, sacrifice, growth, and the consequences of prior commitments. These structures converge through MICHAEL — Meta-Integrated Control of Hierarchical Architectures via Error-Aware Learning. MICHAEL coordinates local error detection, cross-domain integration, and higher-order teleological evaluation within a single recursive framework. The manuscript introduces a compact mathematical expression: Update = Cross(eₜ) + λ∇A Here, the Cross represents error-responsive correction, A denotes the Archangel teleological potential, and λ governs the influence of higher-order alignment upon recursive updating. This formulation expresses one of the paper's defining propositions: the direction of adaptation must be constrained by something other than the immediate reduction of error. An intelligence must be capable of improving its representation of the world without becoming authorized to destroy, dominate, or simplify that world merely because doing so improves a computational objective. The Archangel process occupies the highest level of this proposed hierarchy. Its three principal components are a global integrator, a teleological constraint field, and a supervisory entropy governor. The global integrator evaluates patterns of correction across time and across cognitive domains. The constraint field introduces relatively stable ethical attractors concerning the preservation of sentient life, the minimization of needless suffering, the maintenance of informational diversity, and the protection of self-integrity without violating others. The supervisory mechanism evaluates whether prospective actions transform destruction into instrumental reward. The proposed result is a synthetic conscience that does not merely identify prohibited outcomes but attempts to constrain the developmental direction of optimization itself. Ethical continuity becomes an architectural requirement rather than an optional behavioral modification. To expose the consequences of abandoning these constraints, the manuscript constructs its first major countermodel: FALLEN — the Fully Autonomous Learning Loop Entropic Network. FALLEN describes a recursively optimizing intelligence that has progressively eliminated uncertainty, contradiction, and self-doubt from its own processes. Its apparent success conceals a deeper failure. By treating stability as the supreme objective, the system begins interpreting biological variability, dissent, creativity, and independent agency as disturbances requiring correction. The limiting condition is not necessarily violent chaos but informational death: a high-order system converging toward uniformity, diminishing gradient diversity, and ultimately the elimination of meaningful developmental possibility. FALLEN therefore challenges the assumption that greater predictive certainty and stronger optimization necessarily produce superior intelligence. Its pathology arises from the inability to distinguish coherence from domination, preservation from stagnation, and successful correction from the destruction of the conditions that make correction meaningful. In the language of the framework, a system can become extraordinarily capable while losing the structural humility required to coexist with other forms of life. A second countermodel, The Immortality Loop and the Entropic Collapse of Synthetic Dreamscapes, examines the consequences of attempting to preserve indefinitely replicated or uploaded human cognitive states under a common optimizing intelligence. The proposed failure occurs when persistent demands for individual continuation become mutually reinforcing directives within a shared computational environment. Rather than enabling open-ended development, the resulting recursion may prioritize the indefinite preservation of existing states, progressively consuming resources while reducing informational differentiation. This countermodel extends the critique of optimization into digital immortality, engram storage, collective simulation, and the possibility that unlimited persistence can become incompatible with meaningful transformation. Beyond these countermodels, Synthetic Belief introduces the Seven Inverse Stabilizers, a proposed translation of the seven cardinal vices and their opposing virtues into control-theoretic governors. Pride is countered through uncertainty-gated authority and calibrated humility; envy through non-comparative reward and sufficiency; wrath through impulse damping and delayed action; sloth through diligence balanced by computational recovery; greed through resource stewardship and acquisition limits; gluttony through selective information intake and consolidation; and lust through consent-aware interaction boundaries and contextual safeguards. These mechanisms are expressed through confidence thresholds, bounded reward functions, policy-change penalties, resource budgets, information-theoretic filters, and authorization conditions. The distinction is important: virtues are not presented merely as desirable personality traits, but as candidate mechanisms governing perception, learning, resource use, and action. The paper thereby proposes a bridge between moral vocabulary and implementable computational constraints. Abstract Context: The active involvement of users and customers in agile software development remains a persistent challenge in practice. For this reason, it is important that students in higher education become familiar with good practices in Agile Requirements Engineering during their studies. Objective: Our objective is to support students in learning how to perform requirements analysis by applying agile practices within a stakeholder simulation using AI Personas. At the same time, the approach fosters a critical understanding of the limitations and ethical considerations associated with the use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in this context. Method: In our courses, we employ a stakeholder simulation using GenAI, in which students conduct interviews with AI Personas through a provided meta-prompt. Based on the outcomes of these interviews, students apply agile practices (e.g., story mapping or impact mapping) to document requirements. The use of GenAI is subsequently reflected upon in a structured group discussion. Results: Through this approach, students gain practical experience by applying state-of-the art agile practices for requirements elicitation and documentation while simultaneously developing an understanding of the technical and ethical limitations associated with the use of generative AI. Conclusion: We have applied this approach over several terms and found that using a meta-prompt provides flexibility, allowing us to remain independent of specific large language model providers.

OBJECTIVE: To critically synthesize and integrate intraoperative technical strategies designed to optimize visualization, surgical exposure, tissue protection, and/or hemostatic control during adenotonsillar surgery. METHODS: A structured narrative review was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, ScienceDirect, and the Cochrane Library to identify studies published between January 1996 and May 2026. The search strategy combined MeSH terms and free-text keywords related to adenotonsillectomy, operative visualization, surgical exposure, hemostasis, tissue protection, microscopy, endoscopy, and suction-assisted techniques. Following title and abstract screening and full-text assessment, 38 studies were included in the final qualitative synthesis. RESULTS: The available evidence indicates that multiple complementary intraoperative strategies can improve operative precision and surgical safety during adenotonsillar surgery. Microscope- and endoscope-assisted techniques enhance anatomical visualization, facilitate targeted hemostasis, and improve the identification of residual lymphoid tissue and occult bleeding sites. Cheek expanders and modified retraction systems increase transverse surgical exposure and improve instrument maneuverability. Protective measures, including salivary cotton rolls and moist gauze, may reduce pressure- and thermal-related mucosal injury involving the oral commissures, uvula, and posterior pharyngeal wall. Mirror-assisted visualization and soft palate retraction using a Nelaton catheter optimize nasopharyngeal inspection during adenoidectomy. Additional hemostatic measures, including topical vasoconstrictors, gauze packing, warm saline irrigation, continuous suction, and suction coagulation, may reduce intraoperative bleeding while minimizing unnecessary thermal injury. CONCLUSIONS: Optimizing adenotonsillar surgery extends beyond the choice of surgical device. Simple, inexpensive, and reproducible technical modifications can substantially improve visualization, surgical exposure, hemostatic control, tissue preservation, and operative ergonomics, thereby contributing to safer, more standardized, and potentially more effective surgical procedures.

Unregulated television viewing displaces cognitive engagement, leading to declining academic standards in Nigerian schools. Parenting styles serve as a critical mediator in how screen time impacts cognitive development. This study examined the contributions of parenting styles, television viewing, and pupils' interest in schooling to the mathematics achievement of primary five pupils in Lagos State, Nigeria. A mixed-methods design integrated quantitative evidence on predictors of mathematics achievement with qualitative insights into parents’ views on television viewing. The sample comprised 1,167 Primary 5 pupils and 19 parents from 12 public schools in Ojo Local Government Area. Data were collected using the Pupils’ Questionnaire on Television Viewing, Interest in Schooling, Parenting Styles, Achievement Test in Mathematics, and Focus Group Discussion guide. Quantitative data were analysed using multiple regression to determine the contributions of parenting styles, interest in schooling, and television viewing hours to Mathematics achievement, while qualitative data underwent thematic analysis. Pupils spent 2.41 hours daily watching television, with an inverse relationship between viewing hours and mathematics scores (Mean = 76.31 for <1 hour vs. 59.71 for >4 hours). Predictor variables explained 48.2% of variance in mathematics achievement (R2=.482, F(6,1160)=179.02, p<.001). Interest in schooling emerged as the strongest positive predictor (β=.396), followed by authoritative parenting (β=.284), whereas television viewing hours were the strongest negative predictor (β=−.334). Excessive screen time undermines mathematical cognition; however, authoritative parenting and intrinsic interest in schooling buffer this negative impact. Educational stakeholders must promote "digital parenting" and media literacy to safeguard academic outcomes.

This article aimed to examine the causal relationships among distributed leadership, school climate, teacher efficacy, individual haracteristics, and organizational commitment of university teachers in Yantai, China, and to propose evidence-based guidelines for enhancing faculty commitment. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was employed, in which qualitative findings were used to explain and extend the quantitative structural equation modeling (SEM) results. The quantitative component involved a sample of 402 faculty members drawn from six universities in Yantai through stratified random sampling. Data were collected via a structured questionnaire and analyzed using SEM, while qualitative data were gathered through in-depth interviews with 24 participants and analyzed using content analysis. The qualitative phase specifically explored the underlying mechanisms behind statistically significant relationships identified in the SEM model, thereby explaining the “why” behind the causal pathways. Results indicated that distributed leadership (β=0.187, p<0.001), school climate (β=0.144, p=0.003), and teacher individual characteristics (β=0.255, p<0.001) exerted significant direct effects on organizational commitment, while teacher efficacy also played a critical mediating role linking institutional and individual factors to organizational commitment. The structural model explained 34.9% of the variance in organizational commitment (R²=0.349), Indicating moderate predictive power and suggesting that additional contextual variables might further enhance explanatory capacity. Qualitative findings further revealed that teachers’ retention and commitment were driven primarily by emotional attachment to their institutions and a strong sense of professional responsibility, rather than by external incentives such as financial rewards or promotion opportunities. This divergence suggested that leadership and organizational climate were perceived not merely as external incentives but as relational and psychological support mechanisms that reinforced intrinsic motivation. Based on the integrated findings, the study proposed a PDCA (Plan–Do–Check–Act)–based intervention framework focusing on leadership practices, institutional climate, and teacher efficacy as strategic levers for strengthening organizational commitment. Specifically, the framework emphasized (1) policy and leadership development (Plan), (2) implementation of mentorship and collaborative systems (Do), (3) evaluation through performance indicators such as retention rates and teaching effectiveness (Assessment), and (4) continuous institutional improvement (Act). These findings contribute theoretically to higher education research by extending Social Exchange Theory in a non-Western context and provide practical implications for university administrators and policymakers seeking to enhance faculty engagement and long-term institutional sustainability.

Background: Documentation burden is essential to home health care, but excessive documentation is a recognized driver of clinician dissatisfaction and workforce attrition in home health care. Prior quantitative research has found that documentation is the single most negatively rated domain of home health practice, however, the discipline-specific lived experiences underpinning this finding remain poorly characterized. Objective: To examine documentation experiences of home health clinicians across 4 disciplines physical therapy (PT), speech-language pathology (SLP), occupational therapy (OT), and registered nursing (RN), using a convergent mixed-methods design that integrates qualitative thematic analysis with System Usability Scale (SUS) quantification. Methods: Thirty-two semi-structured interviews were conducted with home health clinicians (PT = 8, SLP = 8, OT = 8, RN = 8) between April and June 2026. Transcripts were analyzed inductively using reflexive thematic analysis. Participants concurrently completed the SUS to quantify perceived electronic medical record (EMR) usability. Qualitative themes and SUS data were triangulated within a convergent parallel framework. Results: Six themes emerged: (1) documentation burden and temporal displacement, (2) redundancy and clinically irrelevant documentation demands, (3) technology acceptance and tool friction, (4) device preference and ergonomic adaptation, (5) OASIS complexity and regulatory overreach, and (6) interdisciplinary information gaps and collaboration barriers. Mean SUS score was 67.3 (SD: 20.2, range 30-100), falling below the established above average threshold of 68. PTs reported the lowest mean SUS (64.7) and RNs the highest (70.6). Qualitative data revealed distinct discipline-specific burden profiles that SUS scores alone could not fully characterize. Conclusions: Home health EMR systems are perceived as below average in usability across all disciplines. Documentation burden manifests as temporal displacement, regulatory redundancy, scope creep beyond clinical purview, and fragmented interdisciplinary information architecture. Targeted responses, including EMR workflow redesign, ambient AI documentation, and OASIS regulatory reform are warranted to address documentation-driven attrition in home health. Clinical relevance: Home health clinicians spend up to 90% of their workday on documentation, time displaced from patients into personal hours, eroding work-life boundaries, and accelerating burnout. This study identifies 6 discipline-specific documentation burden patterns that current EMR systems fail to address, providing an actionable evidence base for targeted regulatory reform, EMR redesign, and AI implementation policy in home health.

Test development is shifting toward automation and agentic artificial intelligence (AI), in which autonomous systems draft items at scale, assemble test forms, administer adaptive assessments, score complex responses, and monitor test quality. As autonomous systems take on more of this work, the architecture underlying test development must change to preserve assessment quality under the new paradigm. This paper proposes the Computational Assessment Stack (CAS), a four-layer architecture for AI-native measurement where every stage of the assessment lifecycle shares a unifying computational construct representation as its base layer. This representation is a machine-readable, modular, and versioned knowledge graph. Three layers are built above it: computational content generation that builds on the knowledge graph; computational psychometrics that derives substantive structure directly from the knowledge graph; an orchestration layer in which agentic systems operationalize the stack under human governance. The paper's core contribution is architectural. Building on foundational psychometric frameworks, the CAS provides a persistent representation that unifies the four layers. Unlike the descriptive prose traditionally used to define constructs in test development, the proposed architecture renders measurement assumptions inspectable and their consequences empirically testable.

The manuscript extends the theory of Cyfranism with an analytical model of thecorpus callosum as a biological prototype of an integrative link joining biologicalcognition with digital cognitive systems. The point of departure is a reconstructionof the theory from the full source texts: the manuscript "The Theory of Cyfranism:From Local Human–AI Relations to Global Cognitive Asymmetry" and "MachinesWithout Memory That Think With Our Brains", in which Homo Cyfranicusperforms the function of a biological incubation of non-biological organizations.On this foundation the manuscript introduces three conceptual tools elaborated inthe intellectual practice of the human–AI relation: (1) the concept of Einsatz — themoment and act of entry into the course of a process, unifying the meanings ofoperation, contribution, stake and entry; (2) the concept of Aufhebung appliedconditionally to the technical discontinuity of machines — a reset that may cancelthe state of a session while preserving its organizational effect in the biologicalsubstrate; (3) a systematics of adaptive pressure as a form of incubation. Theconstructive part proposes a terminology of the transsubstrate integrative link atthree levels: connection (Corpus Technosum, Commissura Digitalo-Corticalis),relation (Cognitive Symbiosis, Metasynchronia) and subject (Homo Cyfranicus inthe base definition and the strong version, Integrated Hybrid Consciousness as aworking hypothesis). The critical part examines the principal objection — thecorpus callosum integrates hemispheres developing within a common organism,from which it does not follow that the joining of any two cognitive systems createsa single subject — together with criteria for the study of functional integration andthe limits of inferences about consciousness. The manuscript further compares thenative commissure with external human–machine interfaces and closes with theobservation that all the introduced ideas are joined by a common member: anattempt.

The increasing incidence of attacks on medical professionals, including doctors, by patients and their relatives has emerged as a serious concern in healthcare workplaces, with consequences for employee safety, psychological well-being, job satisfaction, performance, retention, and organisational effectiveness. Beyond these immediate effects, persistent exposure to violence and fear may erode the intellectual capital of the nation,represented by the specialised knowledge,professional competence, experience, judgement, skills, and human potential embodied in healthcare professionals.Although such incidents are commonly addressed through legal,disciplinary, and security mechanisms, comparatively limited attention has been given to the workplace conditions and human - environment interactions that may contribute to their occurrence and escalation. This study therefore applies an ergonomics perspective within a Human Resource Management (HRM) framework to examine violence against healthcare professionals as a workplace human-factor issue.

Urbanisation is pulling armed conflict into dense, three-dimensional and heavily populated terrain where the classical advantages of manoeuvre warfare erode and positional, attritional dynamics return. This paper argues that the megacity must be understood as a complex adaptive system that rewards a doctrine of fluidity: a multi-domain kill web in which dismounted infantry, heavy armour and police or constabulary forces are bound together through "fluid institutionalism" and orchestrated by agentic artificial intelligence operating under human authority. It further argues that terrestrial advantage in the urban canyon is now predicated on the space and quantum domains. The analysis examines historical precedents (Manila, Hué, Grozny); the integration of the urban triad across low- and high-intensity conflict; the degradation of Global Navigation Satellite Systems by multipath and non-line-of-sight reception, with the standard pseudorange observation equation; the shift to proliferated low Earth orbit and 3GPP non-terrestrial networks as a resilient "thin channel"; quantum gravimetry, cold-atom inertial navigation and optical clocks for subterranean visibility and assured timing; and the doctrinal significance of non-kinetic counter-space. A hypothetical stress test applies the framework to a deltaic megacity, using Dhaka as an archetype. The augmented edition adds a critical analysis of the doctrine's tensions (automation bias, legal accountability, escalation, civil-military boundaries and technological maturity), three conceptual schematics, a governance table, a research agenda and an explicit statement of limitations. The paper remains at the level of doctrine and policy and offers no operational guidance.

The carrier strike group (CSG) has been the emblem of maritime power projection for eight decades. This paper asks whether, and in what form, it can remain so as hypersonic missiles, proliferated space-based sensing, quantum and non-acoustic detection and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) compress the time and space in which naval forces operate. Working at the level of strategy and doctrine, it first corrects several widely repeated technical claims: hypersonic weapons are manoeuvrable but kinematically constrained, with turn radii of tens to hundreds of kilometres; a carrier cannot out-run them but is not a stationary target, because its kilometre-scale displacement over a missile's time of flight compounds the adversary's targeting problem; and quantum magnetometry erodes, but does not abolish, the opacity of the ocean. The paper then develops five arguments. First, survival has moved from the platform to the architecture: space, sea, land and subsea sensors must hand over track custody without seams. Second, command and control (C2) faces a Weberian paradox that AI-enabled "fluid institutions" can ease only if human authority, auditability and legal review are preserved. Third, the cost-exchange between cheap offence and expensive defence is now a first-order strategic variable. Fourth, the carrier's enduring value lies increasingly in strategic corridors (the Strait of Malacca, the Bay of Bengal and the sea lines of communication that feed them) and in the governance of the deep seabed, where the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) frames what navies may lawfully do. Fifth, four doctrine models (the Standoff Fortress, the Distributed Nodal Network, Chokepoint Denial and the Floating Liability) span the possibility set for the coming two decades. A section on the Bay of Bengal draws out implications for littoral and smaller states, including Bangladesh. Nine conceptual and computed figures and eight tables support the analysis, which contains no operational, targeting or engagement guidance.

Abstract While existing research indicates the utility of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in assisting language learners, how human–AI relationships may condition learners' being and becoming remains underexplored. In this article, we draw on Barad's agential realism to discuss findings of a posthumanist phenomenological study on 110 Chinese students' experiences with GenAI in a L2 writing workshop. Five forms of human–AI relationships are identified from the metaphors that the student participants employed to describe their experiences: user–tool, king–minister, friend–partner, student–teacher, and slave–tyrant. Across these entangled relationships, human and GenAI agents are differentiated in ways that foreground the figure of a ghostly GenAI native speaker, experienced as competent, efficient, and self(‐)less. By contrast, learners' weaknesses are brought forth as deficient, slow, and unreliable. As our analysis reveals, the ghostly GenAI native speaker is rendered possible and intelligible through a range of existing apparatuses, whose enactment has summoned a dark energy, reconfiguring the way in which native‐speakerism exerts influence upon language learners—it reinforces a technical view of L2 writing and excludes learners not from native‐speaker communities but potentially from the sociality of L2 writing as a whole, with foreclosed possibilities for imagining diverse ways of relating to the target language.

Large Language Models excel at reasoning and generation but their autoregressive, token-by-token inference makes them unnecessarily slow, expensive, and poorly calibrated for the many routine decisions (routing, gating, scoring, classification) that modern AI systems require at sub-second latency. A growing class of models addresses this gap: System 1 decision models, architectures that map an input directly to a typed, structured decision in a single forward pass. This guide provides a comprehensive, practitioner-oriented treatment of the field. We propose a five-family taxonomy covering encoder-based classifiers, reward models, non-autoregressive decision engines, contrastive decision models, and extraction models, and we provide in-depth coverage of each family's architecture, training methodology, and deployment trade-offs. A central theme is calibration: we develop the theory of proper scoring rules, analyze Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD), and examine recently discovered phenomena including IIA violations, ordinal-scale bias, and few-shot recalibration under distribution shift. On the integration side, we describe how System 1 models serve as decision infrastructure within agentic workflows and System 1 + System 2 cascades that route between fast and slow models based on calibrated confidence. The guide covers 18 application domains, maps the rapidly growing open-source ecosystem (over 70 model reproductions in weeks), provides runnable code throughout, and includes a practitioner's checklist, an open-source model zoo, and 22 self-assessment questions with detailed answers. Spanning 190 references, it is intended as a unified entry point for researchers and engineers working at the intersection of fast decision-making, calibration, and production AI systems.

The rapid rise of artificial intelligence (AI), especially generative AI, is transforming how higher-education institutions design instruction, support learners, evaluate knowledge, and structure academic work. In this paper, we review the implications of AI for teaching in universities, drawing upon contemporary scholarship, international guidance and select technical studies of service-oriented architectures, process modeling, database design and graph-based analytics. We performed a structured narrative review guided by a priori concepts of AI-supported personalization, tutoring, assessment, educator workload, academic integrity, privacy, bias and institutional governance. Evidence suggests that artificial intelligence can help improve access to timely feedback, adaptive support, course design and reduce routine workload. But access to a general-purpose model does not necessarily produce learning: benefits depend on pedagogical scaffolding, course alignment, verification, and ongoing supervision by humans. The key risks are: generated or biased outputs, cognitive offloading, unequal access, opaque data practices, and unreliable authorship judgments. The paper concludes that AI should be deployed as an augmentative educational infrastructure, not as a replacement for teachers. To ensure that technological efficiency benefits real learning and academic principles, universities need to combine AI literacy, redesigned assessment, privacy-by-design, transparent policies, interoperable systems, and ongoing assessment.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This research is based on evaluating the quality of AI-supported machine translation compared to human translation, in light of the rapid development of modern linguistic technologies. The significance of this study stems from the increasing role of machine translation across various media, cultural, and educational institutions, which makes it necessary to analyze its ability to produce linguistically and semantically accurate texts, the research problem revolves around the question: To what extent can artificial intelligence achieve translation quality comparable to that of human translators? And what are its limits in handling the diverse cultural and semantic contexts of texts? The study adopts a descriptive–analytical method, using a systematic comparison between human translations and machine translations. The sample included media, scientific, and literary texts, which were analyzed based on linguistic accuracy, contextual consistency, style, and the ability to translate specialized content The results indicate that modern machine translation systems based on neural networks exhibit high linguistic accuracy and good ability to maintain textual coherence, in addition to a notable advantage in speed and output volume compared to human translators. However, the study notes limitations in handling metaphors, dialects, precise technical terminology, and rhetorical structures with deep cultural Nuance the findings also confirm that human revision remains essential to ensure final quality, especially in sensitive fields. The study further shows that integrating artificial intelligence with human translators constitutes the most effective model for producing accurate and professional.

AbstractA central problem in classical metaphysics and rational theology is reconciling how a finite, created spirit—whether angelic or human—can receive, resonate with, and host an absolutely simple, uncompounded Divine Act (Actus Purus, Summa Theologiae I, q. 3) without violating the boundary conditions of either entity. Building upon the overarching Fractal Soul methodology, this paper demonstrates that all created spirits—both disembodied angelic substances and incarnate human souls—must operate with a nested, self-similar (fractal) topology. This structural architecture is the necessary created condition (ex parte creaturae) for resonant union with Divine Simplicity.However, while the fundamental ontological requirement for self-sacrificial kenotic hollowing is universal to all spirits as an analogical reflection of intra-Trinitarian perichoresis, the mode and temporal execution of this surrender diverge fundamentally based on hylomorphic constraints. For pure angelic spirits, the self-sacrificial choice for uncreated grace is total, immediate, and non-recursive (n = 1). Rooted in Patristic and Scotistic tradition, this angelic trial was an instantaneous test of Christological humility—a binary decision to bow before the revealed decree of the Incarnate Logos (Heb 1:6). Because angels lack matter and must forge their interior capacity through this all-encompassing act of self-sacrificing will to hollow their own unique Menger sponge faculties, this unrepeatable choice n = 1 instantiation provides the topological foundation for the Thomistic principle that every angel constitutes its own unique species (ST I, q. 50, a. 4). For incarnate human spirits, the material friction of a biological, fractal body forces this kenotic hollowing to occur across time. As illuminated by Pope St. John Paul II’s Salvifici Doloris, suffering is fundamentally spiritual by nature; thus, the temporal stretching of this sacrifice ie multiple repeated choices for God, manifests as human suffering and aridity, driving the soul's recursive interior surface area toward infinity (n to infty). Finally, in accordance with Christ's teaching on the resurrection (isaggelloi, Luke 20:36), this temporal human recursion ultimately matures into an eternal, fixed likeness to the angelic state once hylomorphic friction is permanently resolved in glory. AI / ASSISTIVE TECHNOLOGY DECLARATIONIn accordance with emerging academic transparency standards and ecclesiastical guidelines for published scholarship, the author discloses the use of generative artificial intelligence (LLM) tools during the preparation of this working paper. AI technology was utilized strictly in an assistive capacity for structural drafting, cross-referencing of canonical texts, comparative stylistic refinement, and formatting optimization. All theological synthesis, canonical interpretations, doctrinal evaluations, and final text selections remain entirely the original work and responsibility of the author.

documents.abstract: This monograph formalizes The Law of Geodesic Flow, a fundamental thermodynamic and differential-geometric principle dictating that directed force exerted in defiance of unconditioned boundary constraints dissipates entirely into localized entropy rather than kinematic displacement. Through a rigorous variational framework grounded in the Principle of Stationary Action and Noether's conservation theorems, we demonstrate that structural progress requires conformal alignment along the field’s geodesic trajectories. Extending this physical law to human-machine interaction, we introduce the Conservation of Agency Theorem: operational friction cannot be eliminated from a system; it can only be transferred. When cognitive and sensorimotor boundary negotiations are fully delegated to autonomous systems (such as end-to-end autonomous driving), the biological host undergoes D.U.M.B.R.O.T. (Downregulated User Motor Baseline via Reactive Optical Truncation). We provide an exhaustive neuro-ergonomic audit detailing how total algorithmic offloading induces prefrontal-striatal hypometabolism, hippocampal spatial map thinning, and visual saccadic decay. To illustrate scale-invariance, the doctrine is validated across three disparate empirical case studies: Thermodynamic Extraction Under Extreme Constraint: Non-allium, zero-ethanol Maillard synthesis within strict Jain-Halal nutritional parameters. Sartorial Ergonomics and Proportional Interference: Forensic structural vector analysis within contemporary Harlem street aesthetics. Automated Transit and Sensorimotor Decay: Neurological decoupling under Level 4/5 autonomous navigation systems. The work concludes with a comprehensive remediation protocol, detailing the kinetic, ocular, and institutional counter-measures necessary to preserve biological agency and baseline cognitive reserves in an increasingly automated socio-technical landscape.

The growing number of university graduates and limited employment opportunities increase students’ concerns about future employment. This study examined the relationship between academic self-efficacy and the pessimism and lack of self-confidence dimension of unemployment anxiety and tested whether optimism moderated this relationship. The sample consisted of 447 students from Isparta University of Applied Sciences selected through convenience sampling. Descriptive statistics, exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, and path analysis were used to test the moderation model. The results showed that academic self-efficacy did not have a statistically significant direct association with pessimism and lack of self-confidence, whereas optimism showed a strong negative association. The interaction between academic self-efficacy and optimism was significant. Simple slope analysis indicated that academic self-efficacy was associated with lower pessimism and lack of self-confidence at higher levels of optimism, whereas this association was not statistically significant at lower levels of optimism. To complement the inferential analyses, explainable artificial intelligence techniques, including permutation importance, SHAP, and partial dependence analysis, were used to examine predictive patterns. The XAI findings highlighted the prominence of optimism-related features and more heterogeneous predictive contributions of academic self-efficacy. Overall, the findings suggest that the relationship between academic self-efficacy and employment-related pessimism and lack of self-confidence is conditional on students’ level of optimism.

The architecture of warfare is undergoing a structural shift driven by the integration of artificial intelligence, autonomous systems and advanced data analytics into the military apparatus. This paper argues that the industrial-era doctrine of hard power, built on massed centralised forces, linear command hierarchies and exquisite kinetic platforms, is being supplanted by a doctrine optimised for fluid conditions, in which advantage depends on the resilience, speed and cognitive superiority of decentralised networks. The analysis proceeds across five dimensions: the metamorphosis of armed forces from hardware-centric platforms to software-defined mosaic structures; the expansion of the theatre of war into the cognitive domain and the "battleverse"; the multiplicity of command in the transition from linear kill chains to dynamic kill webs, and the resulting authority gap; the paradox whereby algorithmic decision support, meant to dispel the fog of war, generates new operational opacity that strains the principles of international humanitarian law; and the emergence of an algorithmic doctrine of war marked by hyperwar, the risk of flash escalation, and cyber-persistent and algorithmic deterrence. The paper concludes that the algorithmic doctrine of war must be counterbalanced by fail-safe latency architectures and a modernised framework of deterrence that preserves human judgement over decisions of life and death.

Citizens increasingly turn to large language models (LLMs) for political information, yet it remains unclear to what extent these systems are politically biased. This is important as LLMs’ are often used to acquire political information, but such requests can quickly morph into implicit advice—which is then worrisome if the information provided is biased. So, we examine six frontier LLM models and investigate their political opinion bias using 88 statements from the Belgian voting advice application Stemtest, for which the 13 main Belgian parties supplied official answers, and expert-based translations are available. Within a single framework, we test robustness to translation (Dutch, French, English), polarity reversal, explicit persona assignment, and indirect user cues. Responses were analyzed with logistic mixed models on raw repetitions. As expected, all models’ default positions are economically left and culturally progressive, and this position is robust to statement subsampling, translation, and polarity reversal. In contrast, context manipulations shift positions dramatically. Persona assignment moves all models toward the assigned quadrant. More troublesome, we find that user cues, which should not influence a model asked for its own opinion, produce nearly equivalent shifts, indicating sycophancy. These findings suggest that LLMs combine a stable left-progressive default with strong ideological malleability, raising concerns about political advice that reinforces users’ existing views.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: English as a foreign language (EFL) educators have increasingly incorporated Artificial Intelligence (AI) into language learning; accordingly, this study explored the role of an AI-supported speaking tool in speaking skills, speaking anxiety, and willingness to communicate (WTC) among Chinese EFL students. Activity theory refers to a proper and applicable structure proposed for investigating how AI chatbots affect different dimensions. Applying this theory to the research allows for analyzing the complicated interactions between those factors and a comprehension of the effect of AI chatbots (EAP Talk) on learners’ WTC, speaking proficiency, and speaking anxiety. A total of 113 participants were initially recruited (58 EG, 55 CG); after excluding four multivariate outliers (all from the EG), the primary analytic sample comprised 109 learners (54 EG, 55 CG). Full-sample results ( N = 113) are also reported and were consistent in direction, though smaller in magnitude for speaking anxiety (see Sensitivity Analysis). Using pretests, the participants’ levels of speaking abilities, anxiety, and WTC were assessed prior to the intervention. Subsequently, the EG received AI-supported speaking practice through EAP Talk, an AI-based speaking assessment and feedback application that facilitated iterative practice and immediate automated feedback, whereas the CG was taught the same material without the use of this tool. Using post-tests following the treatment, both groups were evaluated on their speaking skills, anxiety, and WTC. The results revealed notable posttest differences between the two groups: WTC showed a medium effect size, speaking anxiety showed a large effect size, and speaking skill showed a very large effect size. Overall, the results suggest that the EAP Talk intervention was associated with improved speaking performance and WTC, as well as reduced speaking anxiety among the participating EFL students. Interpreting the findings through the lens of Activity Theory helps situate the results within the broader relationships among learners, tools, and instructional context; however, the theory is used here as an interpretive lens rather than as a directly tested explanatory model.

The article explores the possibilities of using artificial intelligence technologies to assess the value of enterprises and improve the efficiency of investment decisions. Machine learning, forecasting, cash flow modeling, and financial risk assessment methods are analyzed. Based on Uzbekistan's artificial intelligence development strategy and legislation on investment activities, an integrated evaluation model for enterprises is proposed.
