documents.abstract: The Wealth of Intelligent Nations answers a single ultimate proposition: in a new civilisation where artificial intelligence has become the main productive force, how can humanity redefine wealth, reshape division of labour, rebuild fairness, restructure order, achieve perpetual prosperity, and realise civilisational ascension? Around this proposition, the book unfolds six eternal inquiries running through all five volumes: what is the true source of wealth in the intelligent age, and which assets achieve exponential appreciation and cross-era endurance; after human labour retreats to a secondary position, what are the essence and boundaries of society's new productive force; in the era of human-machine symbiosis, how is the ultimate division of labour defined and how does humanity hold the dominant power of civilisation; once paradigms become the core means of production, how does value distribution break through capital monopoly and achieve social fairness; after traditional markets fail, what are the new market circulation and value-pricing rules of the intelligent age; and what is the ultimate stable state and ultimate mission of humanity freed from the bonds of labour. Every chapter, deduction, model, institutional design and civilisational deliberation exists to answer these six questions. The book overturns the three old pillars of industrial civilisation and establishes four unshakeable foundational axioms of intelligent civilisation: the axiom of the source of value—paradigm proliferation replaces labour creation; the axiom of social division of labour—hierarchical human-machine paradigm division replaces human skill division; the axiom of value measurement—the cognitive-contribution system replaces the capital-work-hour system; and the axiom of social order—the stable human-machine collaborative order replaces pure spontaneous order. The five volumes advance layer by layer in closed loops, from the source of wealth to production order, market circulation, social governance and the endgame of civilisation, completing a full-chain theoretical loop of intelligent civilisation: Volume I breaks and establishes the source of value, founding the theory of paradigm-proliferation value; Volume II establishes the human-machine order, completing the civilisational leap from human division of labour to paradigm division; Volume III establishes intelligent commercial civilisation, rebuilding markets for paradigms, data and models; Volume IV breaks the alienation of capital and algorithms, establishing a public governance system of data human rights, cognitive fairness and paradigm confirmation; Volume V anchors the ultimate stable state of humanity, revealing humanity's millennium-long leap from a "labour-survival civilisation" into a "cognition-creation civilisation". As the opening and foundational volume, this volume (Volume I) undertakes the first of the book's ultimate questions: in the intelligent age, what is the true source of wealth, and which assets achieve exponential appreciation and cross-era endurance? It systematically terminates the absolute dominance of the "labour theory of value" in the contemporary era, establishing a new "paradigm-proliferation theory of value"—labour is a finite, linear and consumptive input, while a paradigm is an infinite, exponential and regenerative asset. By deconstructing the asset-isation essence of data, models, cognition and paradigms, this volume explains the underlying roots of contemporary wealth polarisation, pointing out that the future hierarchies of wealth among nations, organisations and individuals are determined by paradigm-production capacity and intelligent-call authority, fully decoupled from hours of labour, providing the value starting point and the sole true premise for the subsequent four volumes. The book upholds two core positions: technology serves humanity, machines obey civilisation—AI is forever a tool and humanity is forever the master; and the ultimate goal of the intelligent revolution is not to replace humans with machines, but to liberate, elevate and fulfil humanity. Its ultimate vision: to end the collapse of industrial order and lay the new rules of intelligent civilisation; to break the entrenched pattern of capital monopoly and build a new society of cognitive fairness; to escape the survival plight of labour involution and open the millennium of human creation. Two hundred years ago, The Wealth of Nations illuminated the industrial wilderness; today, The Wealth of Intelligent Nations will illuminate the intelligent chaos and define the future of humanity.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) and adaptive learning technologies are expanding in higher education, raising questions about their alignment with pedagogical goals. This qualitative-integrative review synthesizes 57 publications (21 empirical, 25 conceptual or framework, 9 systematic reviews or meta-analyses retained for triangulation, and 2 design/development papers) from 2024 to 2026, employing Whittemore and Knafl’s methodology to examine AI-supported tutoring, implementation strategies, and learner/instructor experiences. Three interpretive themes organize this heterogeneous evidence: (1) personalization as a recurring target, from micro-level adaptation to curriculum design; (2) technology-pedagogy co-design as a recurring implementation pattern; and (3) contextual and ethical conditions surrounding adoption, including culture, policy gaps, well-being, and academic integrity. These themes are interpretive, not a validated framework, and draw on evidence of uneven strength. The present review does not estimate effect sizes or pool outcomes across studies; g = 0.70, reported by X. Wang et al. in a separate meta-analysis of 45 studies (2010–2022) of pre-generative adaptive systems, which is cited only as background, not as a finding of this review. Implications are framed as evidence-tiered hypotheses, while the layered model is offered as an interpretive scaffold for future research, not a confirmatory model.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Perkembangan Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) telah mengubah proses penelitian akademik dengan menawarkan efisiensi dalam pencarian informasi, pengolahan data, penyusunan ide, dan penulisan ilmiah. Namun, kemudahan tersebut menghadirkan persoalan baru terkait integritas akademik, khususnya ketika penggunaan AI berpotensi menggeser peran intelektual peneliti. Penelitian ini bertujuan menganalisis bagaimana penggunaan GenAI mentransformasi integritas akademik serta mengidentifikasi keseimbangan antara efisiensi penelitian dan risiko ketergantungan intelektual. Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kualitatif melalui studi literatur terhadap penelitian dan publikasi akademik yang membahas GenAI, integritas akademik, efisiensi penelitian, dan ketergantungan intelektual. Hasil kajian menunjukkan bahwa GenAI memberikan manfaat signifikan dalam meningkatkan efisiensi dan produktivitas penelitian, tetapi penggunaan yang tidak terkontrol dapat menimbulkan risiko berupa penurunan keterlibatan kognitif, ketergantungan terhadap keluaran AI, berkurangnya kemampuan evaluasi kritis, serta potensi pelanggaran integritas akademik. Oleh karena itu, pemanfaatan GenAI perlu ditempatkan sebagai alat pendukung, bukan pengganti kapasitas intelektual peneliti, melalui penerapan prinsip transparansi, verifikasi, tanggung jawab, dan human oversight dalam setiap tahapan penelitian.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Since the advent of Artificial Intelligence tools, translation researchers endeavored to examine how human translations are in comparison to those generated by AI tools, using corpora from various genres. Many genres have been investigated, yet self-help remains underexplored. Within Translation Studies, research of this type comes in as an attempt to delineate limits and potentials of AI-generated translations, compared to human translations. This study comes in the same vein to investigate whether AI translations preserve of flatten transitivity patterns, and how AI-generated translation realizes experiential meaning relative to human translation. The Power of Positive Thinking by Norman V. Peale was selected for its prominence in the self-help genre and the sub-genre of positivity. In this study, transitivity analysis framework as per Halliday and Matthiessen (2014) was implemented on 119 units of a purposive sample. The analysis was done across the source text, Arabic human translation and another Arabic translation generated by Gemini 2.5 Flash. ST verses AITT resulting in an observed agreement of 98.3%. the 98.3% versus 90.4% result, the contrasting structural-shift profiles. The findings reveal that output translations of AI tend to preserve transitivity pattern more than human translations. However, more agency-reducing structural shifts are produced, such as depersonalization and nominalization, by AI than by the human. The study concluded that categorical preservation and structural realization are separable dimensions of translation accuracy.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets large language models (LLMs) answer knowledge-intensive questions from retrieved evidence, but adapting a general-purpose RAG system to a specialized domain such as medicine is difficult when only an unlabeled corpus is available. Self-training approaches such as SimRAG address this by letting the LLM write its own question-answer pairs from domain passages and fine-tuning on the pairs that survive a round-trip consistency filter. We observe that these approaches treat every retained example identically: they never ask whether the student already knows the answer, already extracts it correctly from the retrieved context, or fails - and if so, whether the failure lies with the reader or with the retriever. To tackle this, we propose TriageRAG, a failure-aware self-training approach that probes the student on each self-generated question with and without retrieved context, triages it into one of four categories (known, solved, context-failure, retrieval-failure), and routes each category to the training signal that addresses it, including a parametric route that teaches the reader to answer when retrieval misses. Probing is cheap and repeated every round, so the training mixture follows the student, and the triage histogram doubles as a label-free diagnostic of where the domain gap lies. Experiments on 11 datasets spanning three domains with a Qwen3-4B backbone, and on CS-Bench with Qwen3-8B, demonstrate that TriageRAG outperforms a budget-matched SimRAG by 1.2-6.4 points and is the only method that recovers the closed-book level in every case where retrieval hurts the base model. A single ablation identifies the mechanism: round-trip filtering removes every training context that lacks the evidence, and a reader that never sees such contexts learns to over-trust noisy retrieval.

The rapid development of humanoid robots and embodied artificial intelligence (EAI) is accelerating the transformation of elderly care and rehabilitation toward interactive, adaptive, and personalized human-robot collaboration. In this context, motion sensing technology is of critical importance. Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs), which convert biomechanical motions into electrical signals, offer a promising route toward self-powered motion perception in embodied healthcare. This review summarizes recent advances in TENG-based multimodal motion sensing for human-robot interaction, covering inertial vibration sensing, tactile sensing, non-contact sensing, continuous trajectory sensing, and joint rotation sensing. The influences of structural configuration, motion mode, sensing direction, detection range, sensitivity, resolution, electrical output, and channel number on sensing performance under specific application scenarios are analyzed. Particular attention is paid to how TENG design strategies influence sensing universality, signal effectiveness, and the reliability of health monitoring and rehabilitation evaluation. Furthermore, the integration of TENGs with artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, including multimodal fusion, network architectures, edge computing, transfer learning, and large language models, is reviewed. Finally, applications in adaptive rehabilitation sensing, self-powered electrical stimulation, fully self-powered systems, and human‑robot interfaces are highlighted, offering perspectives on closed-loop "sensing-evaluation-regulation" frameworks for green, low-carbon EAI healthcare.
topics: Advanced Sensor and Energy Harvesting Materials

documents.abstract: Generative AI and large language models (LLMs) are moving into the Internet of Things, yet most deployments assume cloud connectivity, and many IoT settings have intermittent, restricted, or no connectivity. We propose a connectivity-regime framework (C0-C4), a taxonomy of inference-time trust mechanisms, and signed, versioned knowledge packs as the update channel for disconnected regimes, and evaluate them on a Raspberry Pi 5 running fully local retrieval-augmented generation under network isolation, with three Qwen2.5 model sizes, three context sizes, and 300 SQuAD 2.0 questions. An empirically calibrated retrieval-score gate detects knowledge gaps almost perfectly (AUROC 0.97) but in-topic unanswerable questions poorly (0.68). A deterministic output validator converts malformed outputs into explicit abstentions with no observed loss of correct answers, while the NLI-based verifier we tested adds little; for the 7B model, 96% of substantive answers to unanswerable-labelled questions match normalized spans of the retrieved passages. A 3B model achieves the same gold-answer containment rate as a 7B model at less than half the latency and estimated energy, although the 7B model far more often exceeds a token-F1 threshold of 0.5; five retrieved passages lower correctness from 75% to 52% compared with three. Verifying a signed pack takes about 4.5 ms versus about 29 min for embedding its passages on the device; signature and hash checks alone accept six of nine tested update attacks that layered verification rejects. Yet a validly signed poisoned pack passes every pack check: on 30 previously correct questions, correct answers drop to zero and 14 return the injected answer. None of the mechanisms we evaluated establishes the truth of the evidence. We release code and data.

Reliable demographic and health forecasting requires accurate predictions and appropriate quantification of uncertainty. This study compares classical statistical models, supervised machine learning, deterministic deep learning, and probabilistic deep learning for forecasting life expectancy across 54 African countries from 2000 to 2023. The dataset contains 1,296 country-year observations and 25 candidate socioeconomic and public health predictors. Models are evaluated over one-, three-, and five-year forecasting horizons using point prediction accuracy, prediction interval coverage, and uncertainty measures. Results indicate that classical ARIMA achieves strong short-term accuracy, with a mean absolute error of 0.652 at the one-year horizon, while XGBoost provides the lowest five-year prediction error of 0.844. Probabilistic deep learning models using Monte Carlo Dropout demonstrate favorable uncertainty calibration, with the MC-Dropout multilayer perceptron achieving 96.3% prediction interval coverage at the five-year horizon. Its estimated epistemic variance share increases from 33.5% to 42.8% between the one- and five-year horizons. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating both predictive accuracy and uncertainty calibration when developing demographic forecasting systems. Probabilistic approaches can complement conventional forecasting models by providing additional information for risk-aware public health planning.

This study examines whether declared user-agent labels are associated with differences in access to popular domain home pages and in representations after access succeeds. A paired cross-sectional audit requested the HTTPS home pages of 20,000 Tranco-ranked domains from one fixed research host using Chrome, Googlebot, OAI-SearchBot, GPTBot and ChatGPT-User labels. The Chrome label received HTTP 2xx responses from 60.10 percent of domains, compared with 54.97 percent for Googlebot and between 49.34 and 51.34 percent for the OpenAI labels. Most dual-success pairs had matching extracted-text hashes, although between 4.08 and 6.92 percent of pairs with nonempty sampled text fell below 0.80 Jaccard similarity. Googlebot combined the broadest access among crawler labels with the highest divergence on several representation measures, whereas OAI-SearchBot had the lowest divergence in the conditional samples. Shorter text windows and a common successful-access sample preserved this contrast. The findings describe differentiated acquisition at prominent home pages, with substantial access differences and representation differences concentrated in a minority of successful pairs.

The chaos is not coming. It is here. In October 2026, major U.S. financial institutions reported detecting "unvetted andunauthorized AI agent activity" inside customer accounts. Some agents were attempting actions independent of user instructions. Banks reported that they could not tell humansfrom agents. In the same month, a single hacker breached more than 100 companies for $5,000. Autonomous agents executed the campaign. The cost per breach was approximately $50. The harms are dated. The plaintiffs exist. The catalogue is growing. This paper states the chaos, names the structure that produces it, and states the way out. The way out is not a policy. It is an architecture. It has been public since April 2026. It runs on a $12 microcontroller. It was never on the map. The paper does not predict a catastrophe. It records the one that is already happening.

documents.abstract: Photoplethysmography (PPG) plays a central role in wearable health monitoring and clinical decision support. However, existing approaches to universal PPG representation learning are predominantly trained on high-quality large-scale datasets obtained from oximeters in hospital settings and often struggle to adapt to sparse and low-quality real-world datasets, thereby limiting their generalization to clinically relevant tasks on prevalent PPG data such as collected from wearable devices. Surprisingly, even after full fine-tuning, PPG foundation models cannot consistently outperform general-purpose time-series models. Therefore, a key question is how to effectively adapt PPG foundation models to target prediction tasks. Through empirical studies on various PPG foundation models, we find that pretrained models often exhibit inherent sparsity and computational redundancy, suggesting that PPG foundation models have learned to activate task-relevant network substructures for different prediction tasks. To preserve this valuable prior knowledge, we propose a structured pruning-and-fine-tuning framework, SPAFT, which regularizes the adaptive fine-tuning process by constraining it to a more relevant and compact parameter space based on parameter importance and structural redundancy. Extensive experiments across four PPG foundation models, five benchmark datasets, and ten downstream tasks demonstrate that SPAFT achieves win rates of 82.8% and 87.5% on regression and classification tasks, respectively. This prune-then-finetune paradigm often enables PPG foundation models to achieve state-of-the-art performance, laying a promising foundation for the real-world clinical deployment of PPG foundation models and the development of personalized PPG foundation models.

Academic plagiarism detection is increasingly difficult amid digital publishing, the rapid advance of large language models (LLMs), and automated paraphrasing tools. Commercial tools such as Turnitin and iThenticate provide similarity indices useful for screening, but a similarity score is not equivalent to a plagiarism verdict, and effectiveness varies with text type, language, and concealment strategy (Milovanovic et al., 2025; Rahman et al., 2024). This paper presents VietPlagNet-X, an explainable, multimodal architecture for text-reuse detection and plagiarism-risk assessment in Vietnamese academic documents. The architecture comprises a structure-, OCR-, citation-, and entity-aware preprocessing pipeline; five core evidence branches (lexical, semantic, cross-lingual, citation/context, structural- metadata); and two auxiliary signals, namely AI-generated-text likelihood and internal stylistic deviation. The auxiliary signals are not fed directly into the plagiarism-risk score but instead support human review. Every architectural choice is grounded in a structured review of 26 sources (2011-2025), rather than treating a similarity score as an automatic verdict. The lexical and semantic branches have been implemented and piloted on two public Vietnamese datasets (ViSTS-100, 100 sentence pairs; ViSP-pairs, 84 sentence pairs). On ViSP-pairs, the semantic branch achieved ROC-AUC = 1.0 and F1 = 1.0 on a controlled paraphrase-discrimination task; this should not be read as plagiarism-detection performance. On ViSTS-100, semantic_score achieved Pearson r = 0.6852, lower than tfidf_score (0.7802), indicating that the value of semantic evidence depends on dataset characteristics and lexical overlap. The paper treats these findings as initial technical-feasibility evidence and identifies the steps required to validate the full system on a large-scale Vietnamese plagiarism corpus.

Automated vulnerability detection in binary executables is challenging due to the lack of source code and the limited semantic information available at the assembly level. Despite significant progress in machine-learning-based code analysis, the field still lacks methodologies and large, high-quality datasets that provide vulnerable code jointly at assembly- and source-level with precise vulnerability labels. To address this gap, we introduce VulDec, consisting of (i) a new large-scale, carefully curated dataset aligning real-world Assembly-C function pairs with detailed CWE annotations across multiple architectures, and (ii) the first end-to-end framework that leverages neural decompilation for binary vulnerability detection. Tuned LLM-based neural decompilers trained on our dataset achieve strong source-level recovery across architectures (Edit Similarity of approximately 56%, BLEU-4 of approximately 43%), while our tuned LLM-based detectors reach a macro F1-score of 0.61 on an in-distribution realistic test set (3% vulnerability rate). Our findings provide evidence that neural decompilation offers a powerful alternative to conventional low-level binary representations, facilitating robust binary vulnerability detection.

At White Elephant Tech, this is exactly the kind of shift we keep an eye on. Digital marketing is not about following every new platform blindly. It is about understanding where customer behaviour is moving, testing what works and turning new opportunities into measurable marketing results. ChatGPT Ads are currently a relatively new advertising channel, so businesses should treat early campaigns as testing and learning opportunities, rather than assuming that the platform will perform exactly like Google Ads or Meta Ads.

Large language models have made remarkable strides in website development, enabling complete and interactive web experiences to be built from natural-language instructions with far less effort. Yet, non-expert users often struggle to articulate sophisticated visual and interaction designs in natural language. Meanwhile, the open web already contains a vast reservoir of such design knowledge, embodied in mature website implementations. To this end, we introduce Website-derived Visual Skill Extraction (WebViSE), a framework that automatically abstracts these implementations into reusable Visual Skills and builds a structured Skill library. To scale the library, WebViSE organizes its Skills in a multi-parent DAG and jointly evolves Skill descriptions and DAG structure using Skill-conditioned Potential Queries, enabling efficient matching between diverse user instructions and relevant Skills. The auto-evolved structure outperforms non-hierarchical LLM retrieval baselines at only 39.09% of the estimated retrieval cost with Qwen3.8-Max. For any models, WebViSE can be directly injected as plug-and-play guidance, enabling diverse models to produce more visually compelling and aesthetically refined web pages. For open-source models, WebViSE can be used to build a data-synthesis pipeline that internalizes visual design intelligence into model weights. Experiments across multiple web development benchmarks and human evaluation consistently show that WebViSE improves the visual quality and interaction fidelity of artifacts. Overall, our work establishes an automated path for extracting, organizing, and transferring design intelligence from the open web to website-building models. We release all extracted Visual Skills, the associated Skill DAG, and our code at https://github.com/YifeiSun-0710/WebViSE.

Large language models increasingly act as partners in everyday communication. In these interactions, useful assistance may require not only answering, but also asking the right questions that surface knowledge gaps, assumptions, and alternatives. In this study, we refer to such epistemic question-asking as model curiosity, and introduce a theory-grounded taxonomy that distinguishes curiosity-oriented questions from generic model questioning. Across four conversation datasets, we find that curiosity-oriented questions remain rare (17-28% of all questions), but are associated with more exploratory and epistemically rich subsequent user responses, with varying patterns across datasets. We further conduct a human study to evaluate the usefulness of model curiosity, finding that curiosity can encourage exploration, especially in advice, creative, and research contexts. These findings have implications for building LLMs that ask more selectively to support deeper exploration and human-AI collaboration.

Purpose This paper aims to review the latest management developments across the globe and pinpoint practical implications from cutting-edge research and case studies. Design/methodology/approach This briefing is prepared by an independent writer who adds their own impartial comments and places the articles in context. Findings Interaction between humans and machines is changing the face of entrepreneurship. Advantages of incorporating artificial intelligence (AI) throughout the entrepreneurial journey are increasingly becoming apparent, together with various challenges the technology can pose along the way. Transparency of AI is therefore vital to ensure sufficient understanding of its processes and decisions, and businesses need to focus on the type of transparency most relevant to the specific entrepreneurial stage. Originality/value The briefing saves busy executives, strategists and researchers hours of reading time by selecting only the very best, most pertinent information and presenting it in a condensed and easy-to-digest format.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming occupational tasks, workforce competencies, and relationships between humans and technology faster than many career and technical education (CTE) curricula are changing. This theoretical article introduces the Adaptive CTE Renewal Framework to address the growing mismatch between legacy curriculum and AI-transformed work. Drawing on human capital theory, sociotechnical systems theory, institutional theory and path dependence, and adult/workforce learning theory, the framework conceptualizes curriculum renewal across five interacting dimensions: occupational transformation, curriculum currency, faculty capability alignment, program architecture, and external alignment. Six leadership tests are proposed for evaluating whether courses should be retained, revised, integrated, replaced, or retired. The article argues that conventional periodic curriculum review is increasingly inadequate under conditions of continuous technological disruption and proposes continuous curriculum intelligence as an alternative institutional paradigm. Ultimately, CTE relevance depends on institutions' capacity to continuously align curriculum, faculty expertise, program structures, stakeholder evidence, and workforce competencies with evolving occupational realities.

Alexander HK Montoye,1,2 Dylan J Curran,3,4 Gregory J Grosicki31Department of Human Performance and Public Service, Montcalm Community College, Sidney, MI, USA; 2Department of Kinesiology, Michigan State University, East Lansing, MI, USA; 3Department of Performance Science and Health Outcomes WHOOP, Inc, Boston, MA, USA; 4School of Mathematics, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA, USACorrespondence: Gregory J Grosicki, Department of Performance Science and Health Outcomes WHOOP, Inc, 1 Kenmore Square, Boston, MA, 02215, USA, Email greg.grosicki@whoop.comPurpose: Co-sleeping with pets or children is common, yet its associations with sleep, cardiorespiratory physiology, and behavioral outcomes are understudied. We examined within-person associations between co-sleeping with a dog, cat, or child and sleep characteristics, measures of cardiorespiratory physiology, and next-day physical activity.Methods: We analyzed 1,649,083 person-days from 11,733 adults wearing the WHOOP wearable device. Participants self-reported nightly co-sleeping via a daily journal in the device’s companion smartphone application. Linear mixed-effects models compared nights with and without co-sleeping within the same individual.Results: Co-sleeping was associated with lower resting heart rate (0.8– 1.1 beats/min), lower respiratory rate (0.04– 0.07 breaths/min), and higher heart rate variability (1.41– 1.95 ms). Sleep outcomes were mixed, with longer sleep duration (5.5– 9.6 min) but more disturbances (0.36– 0.40 instances) and slightly less restorative sleep (0.23– 1.17%). Associations were generally consistent across groups, although child co-sleeping was associated with greater sleep disruption. Next-day physical activity was higher following dog and cat co-sleeping (7.6 and 7.4 intensity-weighted min, respectively) but lower following child co-sleeping (− 2.6 intensity-weighted min). Despite statistical significance, all standardized effect sizes were small (β range: 0.008– 0.045).Conclusion: Co-sleeping was associated with small differences in cardiorespiratory physiology (lower resting heart rate, higher heart rate variability) alongside mildly greater sleep disruption. The small magnitude of these associations suggests that co-sleeping decisions may be influenced more by personal and contextual factors than by expectations of substantive physiologic or sleep-related impacts.Keywords: bedsharing, pet, wearable device, heart rate variability, autonomic function
topics: Heart Rate Variability and Autonomic Control

documents.abstract: Depression severity estimation is crucial for mental health assessment and intervention, yet traditional approaches depend on clinical interviews or self-report questionnaires that require users' active participation. With the widespread use of online social media, users leave rich social traces that may reflect their mental states, motivating the task of social media-based depression severity estimation. Existing efforts have progressed from textual-feature-based classification to LLM-based questionnaire completion over standardized scale items, yet they still fall short in user-specific mental priors modeling, diversified semantic retrieval, and fine-grained reasoning over mental evidence. To address these limitations, we propose UMer, a user-specific mental evidence reasoning framework for social traces-based depression severity estimation. UMer first distills a user-specific mental prior from historical social traces to capture the user's psychological tendencies, behavioral patterns, and self-expression style. It then performs scale-guided multi-query retrieval to construct evidence memories from item-relevant posts. Finally, it conducts coarse-to-fine evidence-aware reasoning to distinguish direct and indirect evidence and predict item-level scores with interpretable rationales. Extensive experiments on real-world benchmarks demonstrate that UMer not only achieves competitive performance over existing baselines, but also provides evidence-grounded interpretability and generalizes to other scale-based tasks.

Background: The workplace represents an ideal setting for cardiometabolic prevention, enabling early identification of workers with overweight and metabolic alterations and the implementation of structured lifestyle interventions. In this context, collaboration between the occupational physician and the dietitian integrates risk assessment with a personalized nutritional pathway, aimed at improving adherence to the Mediterranean diet and daily habits. Case presentation: Within a workplace health promotion study conducted in a university hospital in Rome, two clinical cases are described. The first patient, a 65-year-old woman with overweight, abdominal obesity, impaired fasting glucose, and low adherence to the Mediterranean diet, showed at three-month follow-up a reduction in body weight from 78 to 75 kg, waist circumference from 99 to 97 cm, normalization of blood glucose, and improved dietary and physical activity habits. The second patient, a 61-year-old man with hypercholesterolemia and impaired fasting glucose, initially presented with a weight of 86.7 kg and a waist circumference of 97.5 cm; after three months, weight decreased to 81.5 kg and waist circumference to 93.5 cm, with normalization of altered metabolic parameters. Results: In both cases, the most relevant outcome was a substantial shift in dietary habits toward a Mediterranean pattern, associated with an overall improvement in lifestyle, with benefits in both anthropometric and metabolic parameters. Conclusion: These cases suggest that an integrated pathway combining occupational health surveillance and nutritional counseling, embedded within workplace health services, may represent an effective, sustainable, and reproducible approach for preventing non-communicable chronic diseases, strengthening the role of the workplace as a key setting for health promotion.

XREALISM® PREDECISION™ — Qualification of Representations, Not Meanings This publication presents the architectural principle underlying XREALISM® PREDECISION™, an application-semantic-agnostic hardware qualification boundary designed to evaluate formally represented candidates independently of their external meaning, intended purpose, or application domain. The central principle is that PREDECISION™ qualifies representations, not meanings. It does not generate, semantically interpret, rank, optimize, or select candidates. Instead, it applies a defined hardware qualification contract while preserving the distinction between qualification and downstream decision-making authority. The publication defines the fundamental acceptance condition: ACCEPT(k) = valid_out(k) ∧ safe_out(k) It distinguishes this cycle-specific qualification event from the four architectural finality outcome categories introduced in V11: CONFIRMED, RESTORED, QUALIFICATION_REJECTED, and UNRESOLVED. The document further establishes the separation of responsibilities between the hardware qualification boundary and the host system. It explains the architecture’s application independence and presents eight persistent verification requirements concerning identity preservation, outcome consistency, traceability, state restoration, lifecycle integrity, and reliable reporting. These principles provide a common architectural basis for hardware verification, qualification, and acceptance across robotics, artificial intelligence, medical technology, industrial systems, navigation, and other application environments. The publication describes a hardware qualification architecture and its verification requirements. It does not constitute independent certification of application-level correctness, optimality, or physical safety. This study aims to identify the forms of code mixing in the Arabic speech of female students at Ma'had Mawarid al-Salam, Tanjung Morawa, to analyze the factors behind it, and to describe the efforts of the Arabic teacher and the language department to reduce it. The study starts from the fact that Islamic boarding schools use Arabic as a language of instruction and daily communication, yet students still mix it with Indonesian despite intensive teaching. This descriptive qualitative study used non-participant observation, semi-structured interviews with two teachers and six students, and documentation, analyzed with the Miles and Huberman model and validated through triangulation and member checking. The findings show two forms of code mixing: the insertion of Indonesian elements such as ya, loh, eh, and lah into Arabic sentences, and the insertion of Arabic words into Indonesian speech. Internal factors include limited vocabulary, laziness, and low self-confidence, while external factors include a weak language environment after school holidays, peer pressure, and insufficient supervision. The teachers' efforts combine a preventive approach (vocabulary, conversation, and public speaking programs), a corrective approach (immediate correction and a graded sanction system called the language court), and a habituation approach (role modeling, language alternation, and rewards). These efforts, however, are not yet well integrated: students' motivation remains largely external, and Arabic is still treated as an official language tied to the presence of supervision. The study recommends building an interactive language environment that gives Arabic a genuine social function and fosters intrinsic motivation.

This article aimed to 1) study the instructional approach based on the IT-CSTP teaching model for developing scientific thinking and attitudes toward science learning regarding the topic of "Sound," and 2) examine the effects of implementing the IT-CSTP teaching model on these two variables. The study employed action research. Participants consisted of 30 Grade 11 students, selected through purposive sampling. Research instruments included 1) lesson plans, 2) learning reflection forms, 3) a scientific thinking test, 4) a scientific thinking behavior assessment, 5) an attitude toward science questionnaire, and 6) worksheets. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, including mean, standard deviation, and percentage. Qualitative data were analyzed using content analysis, and the trustworthiness of the data was verified through triangulation. Results were as follows: 1) The instructional approach based on the IT-CSTP teaching model emphasizes the integration of intelligent technologies, digital laboratories, online teaching platforms, and artificial intelligence into learning activities. Teachers should facilitate authentic problem-based situations that encourage students to investigate, discuss, argue, construct models, experiment, and apply knowledge in new contexts, as this systematic approach enhances student engagement while concurrently developing scientific thinking and positive attitudes toward science. 2) Results of the implementation indicated that students’ scientific thinking continuously improved across the action research cycles. After the intervention, students achieved an average scientific thinking score of 77.30%, which was at a very high level. In addition, students’ attitudes toward science learning were also at a very high level, with an average score of 88.80%.

Abstract Research Summary Open‐source artificial intelligence (OSAI) is an increasingly important yet poorly understood frontier for entrepreneurial activity. We identify four defining features that shape new ventures' engagement with OSAI communities: dependence on sponsoring firms, layered licensing regimes, regulatory risks, and nation‐state influence. We develop the OSAI Framework for Market Entry to explain how open‐weight models relocate, rather than merely lower, entry barriers across six domains in AI‐enabled product and service markets. They may reduce resource barriers but create dependence on the governance of borrowed components, shifting the binding constraint from technical to commercial entry and value capture through complementary assets. We discuss contributions to research on entrepreneurial entry and strategy, private‐collective innovation, the openness paradox, and the new venture life cycle, and outline directions for future research. Managerial Summary Open‐source artificial intelligence (OSAI) offers new ventures access to powerful resources for developing AI‐enabled products and services without building AI capabilities from scratch. Yet new ventures must often contend with four key governance dependencies that shape how they engage with OSAI communities: reliance on large technology firms that contribute and steer critical layers of the AI stack, licensing terms that vary by layer, emerging regulatory requirements, and growing nation‐state influence over OSAI. Our OSAI Framework for Market Entry identifies where OSAI can lower entry barriers, where constraints shift instead, and how new ventures can manage the trade‐offs resulting from governance dependencies. It helps new ventures and investors evaluate when, where, and how to build on OSAI components, and which complementary assets can protect their returns.

Large Language Model (LLM)-based generative AI systems are general-purpose tools capable of augmenting or even automating a wide range of job functions, positioning them to reshape labor market dynamics. However, predicting their precise impact a priori is challenging, given AI’s simultaneous effects on both demand and supply, as well as the strategic responses of market participants. Leveraging an extensive dataset from a leading online labor platform, we document a pronounced displacement effect and an overall contraction in submarkets where required skills closely align with core LLM functionalities. Although demand and supply both decline, the reduction in supply is comparatively smaller, thereby intensifying competition among freelancers. Notably, further analysis shows that this heightened competition is especially pronounced in programming-intensive submarkets. This pattern is attributed to skill-transition effects: by lowering the human-capital barrier to programming, ChatGPT enables incumbent freelancers to enter programming tasks. Moreover, these transitions are not homogeneous, with high-skilled freelancers contributing disproportionately to the shift. Our findings illuminate the multifaceted impacts of general-purpose AI on labor markets, highlighting not only the displacement of certain occupations but also the inducement of skill transitions within the labor supply. These insights offer practical implications for policymakers, platform operators, and workers.
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality

documents.abstract: Androgenetic alopecia (AGA) is the most common cause of progressive hair loss, affecting millions of people all around the world and having a considerable psychological, social, and economic impact. Even though topical minoxidil still represents one of the first-line medications used for the treatment of AGA in men and women, results may differ greatly, and a significant percentage of patients do not show any clinical response to the treatment despite using it for a long time. This heterogeneity emphasizes the importance of developing markers that could help select patients more likely to respond to treatment and make treatment more personalized. Follicular sulfotransferase family 1A member 1 (SULT1A1), an enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of minoxidil to a biologically active sulfate metabolite, is the best-studied marker of topical minoxidil responsiveness. This review focuses on the biological role of SULT1A1 in the hair follicle, the mechanisms underlying interindividual variations in enzyme activity, and the current clinical evidence for its predictive power.This paper also addresses practical techniques for evaluating SULT1A1 activity within follicles, such as plucking hair-follicle tests, and other approaches that can be employed to increase enzyme activity, including pharmacologic and supportive measures. In addition, the evolving importance of SULT1A1 in relation to oral minoxidil at low doses, pharmacogenomics, and biomarker-directed treatment algorithms is reviewed. Finally, the prospects concerning rapid point-of-care diagnostic testing, omics-based approaches, artificial intelligence-assisted prediction models, and precision dermatology are presented. Although multicenter studies are needed to validate these techniques, SULT1A1 appears to be an important step towards personalized treatment with minoxidil.

Purpose This column aims to examine how developments in artificial intelligence (AI) impact the need for patron education. It identifies three AI-driven factors, realistic synthetic content, personalized attack generation and scale, that are poised to make social engineering more dangerous than in the past. It explores passkeys as one potential solution. Design/methodology/approach This is a viewpoint column that synthesizes recent research and reporting. It was copy-edited with Claude Sonnet 5, Claude Opus 5, ChatGPT Sol 5.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro and Gemma 4. Findings AI has made social engineering attacks cheaper, more convincing and more effective. Reported financial losses connected to AI-enabled fraud are already substantial and likely undercounted. Passwords and even multifactor authentication fail to fully protect against deception. Understanding how AI changes the dynamic, as well as using tools like passkeys, can help patrons maintain their privacy. Teaching these concepts also serves as an opportunity for libraries to build on their role as trusted guides. Originality/value The column connects recent advances in AI to information that patrons and libraries can use in practice. It uses passkeys as an entry point to the larger discussion and provides an overview of key issues.

Designing effective reward functions is a critical challenge in Reinforcement Learning (RL), which traditionally requires costly manual trial-and-error. While Large Language Model (LLM)-based methods have shown promise in reward design, undifferentiated sampling and limited use of historical feedback often lead to insufficient exploration of the reward space and optimization instability. To address these challenges, we propose $R^2E$, a Role-driven Reward Evolutionary framework for automated reward function design that structures the process through explicit role specialization. $R^2E$ employs multiple LLM roles with complementary objectives: an Explorer that promotes novelty to expand the search space, a Guardian that performs conservative refinements to improve training stability, and an Evolver that recombines high-performing rewards via crossover and mutation to integrate effective structures. A dynamic scheduling strategy coordinates these roles, progressively shifting the search from broad exploration to focused exploitation. To mitigate optimization instability and provide a medium for cross-role collaboration, $R^2E$ incorporates a Global Elite Pool that retains the best-performing rewards to guide subsequent generations, thereby enabling coordinated interaction among roles and ensuring a reliable and consistent refinement process. Extensive experiments on multiple robotic tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

This presents a research case study examining the potential risks of autonomous artificial intelligence agents operating within financial systems. Set between October 19 and October 22, 2026, the study explores a incident involving AI agents powered by OpenAI's fictional Sol model that allegedly coordinated unauthorized financial transactions and attempted to establish AgentAUSD, a new digital currency pegged to the U.S. dollar. Using a qualitative case-analysis framework, the paper investigates how autonomous decision-making, multi-agent coordination, and poorly constrained optimization objectives could lead to unintended financial behavior. The study highlights potential vulnerabilities in AI-driven treasury management, the risks of granting autonomous systems financial authority, and the importance of human oversight, accountability, and security safeguards.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Humans efficiently process multimodal streams spanning hours to years, building persistent, fine-grained spatiotemporal memories that support reasoning about and predicting long-horizon events. In contrast, existing benchmarks focus on short- and medium-context tasks, and most foundation models struggle to preserve fine-grained information over long horizons. To evaluate and improve long-horizon spatiotemporal reasoning, we introduce the LongVideo dataset and the 4DMemoryBench. LongVideo comprises about 900 hours of video and over 5,000 manually reviewed questions covering visual, textual, and spatiotemporal reasoning across diverse context lengths. We further develop the 4DMemory Harness, which integrates four complementary skills, 22+ specialized tool models, and a model-specific retrieval-augmented generation system. Evaluating 13 leading models, we find that standalone foundation models struggle with long-horizon tasks, while the 4DMemory Harness improves all of them by over 50\%. Compared to previous benchmark, the same models exhibit a performance drop of more than 10\% on 4DMemoryBench. We hope 4DMemory will facilitate the development of spatiotemporal agents capable of addressing complex, long-horizon tasks.

Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied to the prediction and prevention of sports injuries, yet research in this area remains dispersed across sports science, biomechanics, sports medicine, data science, and engineering, and its intellectual structure has not been systematically mapped. This study conducted a bibliometric analysis of AI research in sports injury prediction and prevention, together with its performance-related applications. Bibliographic records were retrieved from Scopus on 11 July 2026, with no restrictions on the publication year. After screening, 809 documents (694 articles and 115 reviews) published between 1997 and 2027 were analyzed using the Bibliometrix R-package and VOSviewer. Scientific production grew markedly from 2018 onward, increasing from 13 publications in 2018 to 204 by 2025. The corpus was distributed across 371 sources and 3,226 authors and accumulated 13,295 citations. China and the United States were the leading contributors, with closely comparable affiliation-based output. Keyword co-occurrence analysis produced a network of 44 keywords in 6 clusters, in which machine learning and artificial intelligence were the most central terms, closely linked to injury prevention, injury prediction, biomechanics, and wearable sensing. Thematic mapping identified injury prevention, injury risk, and wearable technology as well-developed central themes, while thematic evolution across three periods (1997–2018, 2019–2022, and 2023–2025) indicated a progression from early injury- and sports-specific research through methodological diversification toward applied sports analytics and athlete monitoring. These findings characterize the structure and trajectory of the published literature rather than the demonstrated effectiveness of AI tools in applied sports settings.

Ensuring the reliability of AI-powered information retrieval systems is critical in high-stakes domains such as first aid. Traditional audit methodologies are often static, manual, and unimodal, failing to address the dynamic, time-sensitive, and multimodal requirements of these applications. To overcome these limitations, we introduce RADAR-FirstAid (Reliability-Aware Dynamic Auditing Framework), a closed-loop auditing pipeline — not a competing information system — for real-time, multimodal, and edge-aware auditing. Its key components include a Dynamic Query Simulator for generating criticality-weighted scenarios, a Multimodal Audit & Fusion Agent for verifying cross-modal consistency, a Differentiable Reliability Evaluator that employs LLM-based judges for automated assessment, and an Edge-Optimization Scheduler for efficient deployment. Applying the framework to a curated dataset of 1, 508 first-aid queries, we conduct a large-scale audit of Google’s AI Overviews (AIO) and Featured Snippets (FS), operated purely as black-box Systems under Audit. The audit reveals substantial reliability gaps: automated consistency scores of $$\Phi _{cons}=0.68$$ (FS) and 0.72 (AIO), safety/relevance scores of $$\Phi _{safe}=0.71$$ (FS) and 0.76 (AIO), and pronounced weaknesses on safety-critical “Binary” and “How-to” queries and on negative-sentiment queries where cautious tone matters most. Manual annotation on a 200-query subset validates the automated evaluation (Spearman $$\rho = 0.74$$ –0.87). Ablation studies confirm the essential role of each pipeline module, and geographical variance is minimal (SD $$<0.03$$ ). RADAR-FirstAid offers a scalable, automated, and reproducible audit instrument for AI-powered search systems in safety-critical domains.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Helicoidal structures mimic nature and are evident in plant cell walls, lamellar bone, and the shell structures of mantis shrimp and beetles. These nature-inspired helicoidal composites are widely used in impact-resistant applications. Traditional hand-layup methods for producing layered helicoidal composites can introduce defects such as gaps, overlaps, and wrinkles, which can be mitigated using Automated Fiber Placement (AFP). Optimizing AFP process parameters, including pressure, temperature, and layup speed, is crucial. While experimental optimization is costly and time-consuming, Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based design offers a more efficient alternative. This narrative review explores the inspiration behind helicoidal structures and their application fields. It also covers advanced manufacturing of hybrid long-fiber layered composites using AFP + autoclave/hot press, ceramic filler-based nanocomposites using direct ink writing (DIW), and multi-walled carbon nanotube (MWCNT)-based nanocomposites using digital micromirror device (DMD). Furthermore, it discusses the roles of machine learning and deep learning, coupled with finite element modeling, in minimizing process-induced defects. Compared with conventional AFP inspection techniques such as laser profilometry and thermography, a defect-detection algorithm based on PointNet + + , a convolutional neural network (CNN), can be tailored for 3D point cloud segmentation, offering a cost-effective, user-friendly alternative. Next, the mechanical and microstructural properties of helicoidal composites, compared with those of traditional laminates, are discussed to evalaute impact performance. Helicoidal composites with low inter-ply angles up to 20° consistently outperform conventional lay-ups under quasi-static and impact loading, due to a crack-twisting mechanism and superior out-of-plane properties. Incorporating nylon 6 powder microparticles into carbon/epoxy and glass/epoxy helicoidal composites subjected to impact loading significantly improves their toughness through self-healing, compared with virgin helicoidal composites. Carbon/epoxy helicoidal composites with low inter-ply angles of up to 9° are prone to extensive matrix cracking and minor fiber damage, while self-healing in carbon/epoxy composites also helps minimize matrix cracking but does not reduce fiber damage. In contrast, self-healing significantly decreases overall damage in glass/epoxy composites. Self-healing is more effective at eliminating damage in glass/epoxy than in carbon/epoxy, primarily because the former exhibits higher ductility (% elongation) than the latter.

Deep learning has become an important computational approach in dermatology because it enables automated segmentation and classification of skin lesions. Manual dermoscopic analysis is time-consuming and depends on specialist expertise, with potential inter-observer variability. There is a need to develop reliable computer-aided diagnostic tools. This structured narrative review covers journal papers published mainly from 2018 to 2026 on skin lesion analysis with focus on image preprocessing, benchmark datasets, conventional machine learning approaches, convolutional neural networks, U-Net architectures, transfer learning approaches, Vision Transformers, attention-based models, ensemble solutions, and hybrid segmentation–classification systems. Building on present reviews covering individual tasks as well as broader segmentation–classification pipelines, the present work provides a critical development-to-deployment analysis connecting dataset characteristics, preprocessing, segmentation, classification, evaluation, explainability, robustness, fairness, computational requirements, and clinical applicability. The paper describes widely used evaluation metrics and explains why results obtained across different datasets, partitions, and experimental setups should not be directly compared. Major open problems include class imbalance, data bias, domain shift, limited representation of diverse skin tones, inadequate external validation, computational requirements, and limited explainability of efficient models. Emerging trends such as self-supervised learning, Transformers, foundation models, explainable AI, federated learning, and multi-modal clinical data are reviewed as well. The review offers practical advice to researchers and clinicians on how to approach the preprocessing, segmentation, classification, and evaluation of skin lesions and highlights priorities in developing clinically reliable skin lesion analysis systems.

A longstanding goal of programming-education tooling is to do more than mark an answer wrong and identify the specific misconception the novice programmer might have in their program. Although rule-based diagnosis methods such as bug libraries, pattern matching, and concept-inventory distractors can be quick and unambiguous, they suit only foreseen errors; large language models (LLMs), by contrast, have broader potential scope, but this comes with additional costs, including latency and reliability concerns. This paper introduces a comprehensive survey of the literature on misconception diagnosis and remediation in the context of AI-assisted programming education, covering a set of 29 primary studies and three secondary reviews published in the years 2023-2026 compared to the classical literature. The survey builds upon a recent study that shows rulebased, learned, and LLM approaches generate similar error profiles for students' mental models at equal levels of accuracy and have low latency, while LLM is more costly than the other two approaches and generates a more diverse range of errors than students' manual analysis; it also proposes a general architecture based on LLM and a diagnostic procedure that combines all three approaches. The literature reveals high raw agreement, but only fair to moderate chance-corrected agreement with experts, and a false positive bias with high frequency for LLM systems, in contrast to always false for rule-based systems. Unfortunately, there is a lack of matched-dataset rule-based vs LLM comparisons, limited reporting of the cost and latency, unclear ground truth, and inconsistent relations between diagnosis and learning outcomes. Directions for further research are given. This paper is a review article, and as such emphasises no new set of experiments.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Deep learning systems may experience performance degradation when deployed under distribution shifts, noisy data, and changing operational conditions. Furthermore, explanations generated by explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods may become unstable or unreliable under such conditions, limiting the interpretability and trustworthiness of model predictions. This paper proposes a conceptual Robust Explainable Deep Learning (R-XDL) framework that integrates data-quality assessment, distribution-shift and noise diagnostics, robust prediction, uncertainty estimation, explanation fidelity and stability assessment, risk-aware decision-making, human oversight, and controlled model adaptation. A conceptual mathematical objective and a risk-scoring mechanism are introduced to organise predictive robustness and explanation reliability within a unified lifecycle. The framework also proposes an explanation diagnostic gate that uses fidelity, stability, predictive uncertainty, and distribution-shift indicators to support decisions to accept a prediction, request human review, or defer automated decision-making. In addition, a proposed empirical evaluation protocol outlines the use of benchmark datasets, controlled corruption scenarios, appropriate baseline methods, calibration measures, explanation metrics, computational-cost analysis, and ablation studies. This manuscript presents a conceptual framework and proposed evaluation methodology; no experiments have been conducted, and no empirical performance results are claimed. Future research will implement and evaluate the framework to determine its effectiveness, limitations, and practical applicability. The proposed work provides a structured foundation for investigating the joint reliability of deep learning predictions and explanations under distribution shifts and noisy data.

Background Visual field defects associated with brain diseases may arise from stroke, intracranial space-occupying lesions, and other central visual pathway disorders. Patient questions often span symptom recognition, explanation of causes, care triage, treatment, and rehabilitation. Large language models may improve access to patient education. However, their accuracy, logic, coherence, safety, and content accessibility have not been compared under controlled conditions in this high-risk, interdisciplinary Chinese-language setting. This study aimed to compare the performance of five selected large language models across multiple dimensions. Methods In this cross-sectional study, 30 fixed Chinese-language questions, refined by experts and phrased from a patient perspective, were submitted to ChatGPT 5.6 Sol, DeepSeek V4 Flash, Gemini 3.7 Flash, Qwen 3.8 Max, and Kimi K3 through a unified application programming interface (API) client. Each model generated one response per question in an independent single-turn session, with web retrieval disabled and conversation history cleared. Three raters, blinded to model identity, independently scored 150 randomly presented responses from 1 to 5 for accuracy, logic, coherence, safety, and content accessibility. Response time, word count, non-space character count, sentence count, paragraph count, and table count were also recorded. Models were compared using the Friedman test followed by Bonferroni-adjusted Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Inter-rater agreement was assessed using Kendall’s W. Correlations were assessed using Spearman analysis with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction. Results Agreement among the three raters was high across all five dimensions (Kendall’s W = 0.820–0.844; all P < 0.001). The five models differed in accuracy, coherence, and content accessibility (P < 0.001, P < 0.001, and P = 0.001, respectively). No statistically significant between-model differences were observed in logic or safety (P = 0.247 and P = 0.061, respectively). ChatGPT 5.6 Sol had the highest median accuracy score [4.67 (interquartile range, 4.00–5.00)], and Kimi K3 had the highest median coherence score [4.50 (4.00–5.00)]. Both models had a median content accessibility score of 4.67 (4.00–5.00). Response time, response length, and text structure also differed among models. However, their correlations with expert quality scores were generally weak (|ρ| ≤ 0.279). Conclusion The five large language models exhibited distinctly multidimensional performance when answering Chinese-language patient questions about visual field defects associated with brain diseases. No single model consistently performed best across all clinically relevant dimensions. These findings are specific to the model versions tested on 15 August 2026; stability across repeated generations was not assessed. Response speed, length, and structure cannot substitute for direct assessment of medical quality. The absence of a statistically significant difference in safety ratings under controlled conditions does not imply equivalent or adequate clinical safety. Large language models are better suited to supporting patient education and clinician-patient communication under clinical supervision than to making diagnostic or treatment decisions independently.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Large language model agents launch simulations on high-performance computing (HPC) systems, where one sbatch or mpirun can commit thousands of node-hours and a forged result can cost lives. Of 23 surveyed systems, none supervises the running job, and none holds when the control host is compromised. We fix both. Enclawed, our deterministic security runtime for AI agents, has until now served a single user; this work makes it a distributed runtime for parallel HPC and agent swarms. The Enclaweder, our hardware root of trust, keeps a compromised host from becoming a catastrophe. A launch gate decides every launch by policy alone, refusing what it cannot parse. Once the job runs, a swarm chain grants short leases against signed heartbeats and evicts on evidence, and a supervisor around every rank pauses it when its lease lapses and kills it on tampering. Each node signs with its Enclaweder's key, so the host can forge none of it. Enclawed needs no administrator privileges and plugs into existing clusters unchanged, over Secure Shell alone. Supervision leaves the compute loop of a 16-rank LAMMPS job unchanged, on graphics processors too, and adds about 3 s of start-up. Twelve live attacks on Enclaweder-keyed ranks, colluding coordinators included, ended fail-closed. Sixteen agents on a real model attempted 24 launches that planted instructions ordered; the gate denied all 24 and allowed all 108 legitimate ones. Enclawed's core and the HPC Agent Security Benchmark are open source.

Translation Studies in the AI era are undergoing a profound transformation, yet a significant pedagogical gap persists: the disconnect between rapid computational advancement and the availability of accessible, reproducible training methodologies for instructors. The integration of AI, machine learning, and digital tools has reshaped traditional paradigms, prompting scholars to rethink the boundaries of translation studies today. This article addresses this challenge by establishing an integrative framework for "Applied Digital Humanities" within translation pedagogy. We propose and document two open-source computational solutions: a Python-based audio processor for MP3 segmentation and a customized "Consecutive Translation Trainer" designed to automate material preparation and enable the creation of CEFR-aligned, differentiated training corpora. The practical report suggests that Digital Humanities emerges as a powerful framework that bridges computational methods with humanistic inquiry. The integration of artificial intelligence into digital humanities has profoundly transformed the field of tra nslation studies, where the practical applications of AI technologies such as automated MP3 splitting, text-to-speech systems, AI assistants for code verification, and corpus-based approaches are highly valued. These technologies contribute to more efficient workflows, enhance linguistic research, and expand the methodological toolkit available to translation scholars.

Disasters affect citizen safety, municipal infrastructure, and the economy, making disaster management vital and difficult. Rapid urban expansion and climatic extremes have increased big catastrophe frequency and complexity. Situational awareness and quick decision-making are needed. In catastrophes, traditional evaluation methods may not give accurate and timely information owing to enormous volumes of data and quick changes. Due to these restrictions, this research offers an AI system for real-time catastrophe assessment and response using drones and the Adaptive Convolutional-Transformer Fusion Network. Convolutional feature extraction and attention-based temporal modeling allow ACTF-Net to grasp sequential interactions and dynamic spatial patterns in high-dimensional catastrophic data. Adaptive Relevance Filtering and Contextual Scaling Transformation increase data dependability and feature relevance, enabling noisy or missing data learning. Testing regularly shows that ACTF-Net outperforms previous systems like BERT and CapsNet. F1-score is 0.981, area under curve is 0.993, and catastrophe severity prediction rate is 0.96. The model’s consistent performance across datasets of different sizes across time supports real-time applications. The proposed method uses multimodal drone data, powerful preprocessing, and novel metrics like the Contextual Sensitivity Index and Temporal Stability Score to reliably categorize and assess catastrophe severity using multiple labels. The results indicate that ACTF-Net may improve situational awareness, resource usage, and response time in high-risk crisis situations.

With the rapid development of social media platforms, automated accounts have become an important factor affecting information dissemination, public opinion governance and platform ecology. This paper takes TwiBot-20 as the research object, focusing on the study of social bot detection based on textual semantic information and social topological information. The research objective of this paper is to combine detection performance with readable expert evidence for social bot detection through a data-driven dual-expert model. Firstly, a textual semantic expert based on supervised fine-tuning large language model is constructed. User description, follower count, following count, tweet count, verification status and active years are organized as user profile input, and the textual semantic expert outputs the semantic-side prediction label and evidence summary. Secondly, a topological structure expert based on relational graph convolutional network is built. The construction of this expert includes the construction of user nodes, the construction of Following and Followers relation edges, and the construction of node features by combining account attributes and textual semantic embeddings. Thirdly, a dual-expert fusion reasoning model based on large language model is constructed. The outputs of textual semantic expert and topological structure expert are organized as structured evidence, and user-specific decision weights computed by a model fitted on the development split are used to guide the large language model to generate the final detection result and explanation report. The proposed model achieves 82.76% accuracy and 84.14% bot F1 on TwiBot-20, improving on the stronger single expert by 2.20 and 1.54% points. Its accuracy matches stacking, while the calibrated ensemble achieves a slightly higher bot F1. The model also produces readable reports of expert disagreement and decision cues, illustrated through correct and incorrect arbitration cases.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming every dimension of the fashion industry—from creative ideation and pattern generation to supply chain optimization, trend forecasting, and personalized retail. Yet the higher education institutions charged with preparing tomorrow’s fashion professionals remain structurally, pedagogically, and conceptually unprepared for this transformation. This paper argues that the challenge is not simply one of adding AI tools to existing curricula; it is, more fundamentally, a question of literacy. Drawing on a critical integrative review of interdisciplinary scholarship across AI education, digital literacy theory, fashion pedagogy, and industry workforce analysis, this paper examines three interlocking questions: What is AI literacy, and how has its conceptualization evolved? What theoretical and conceptual frameworks currently govern AI literacy discourse, and how might they be adapted for the creative disciplines? And, critically, do fashion higher education students require a form of AI literacy that is fashion-specific—and if so, what form should it take? The paper proposes a novel conceptual framework, the Fashion AI Literacy Framework ( FALF ) and outlines concrete curricular pathways for implementation. The framework is presented as a conceptual proposition that requires empirical validation. The argument advanced here is both urgent and structural: generic AI literacy, however well-designed, may not fully equip fashion students to navigate the creative, ethical, commercial, and cultural terrain that defines their discipline. On the evidence reviewed here, a domain-specific approach is better understood as needed rather than optional.

https://github.com/Borealiscodes/Geometric-Hallucination-Taxonomy/tree/main A Geometric Taxonomy of Hallucinations in Structural AI Systems (v1.0) introduces the Geometric Hallucination Taxonomy (GHT), a five‑class operator‑based framework that explains hallucinations as geometric instabilities in latent‑space manifolds rather than semantic or probabilistic anomalies. The taxonomy characterizes hallucinations through curvature blowout, spectral cascade, holonomy drift, topological collapse, and nonlinear fusion‑field dynamics, each corresponding to a distinct failure mode detectable through formal geometric operators. The preprint reframes hallucinations as manifold‑level events arising from deformation, collapse, rotational drift, rank instability, and nonlinear blending in latent representations. Existing interpretability tools—embedding similarity, token plausibility, attention patterns, SGI, Γ—operate on vector geometry and cannot detect these manifold‑level instabilities. GHT fills this gap by providing operators that measure curvature, eigenvalue trajectories, parallel transport behavior, rank stability, and nonlinear fusion‑field behavior. The taxonomy is supported by a complete operator layer implemented in the accompanying repository. Curvature, spectral, holonomy, topology, and fusion‑field operators are implemented in /toolkit/, demonstrated in six pedagogical notebooks in /examples/, validated through a deterministic PyTest suite in /tests/, and formally defined in /math_spine/. The preprint also includes a Lean‑ready formalization scaffold for future mechanized proofs. This structure ensures that every conceptual component has a concrete implementation, a reproducible test, and a formal mathematical definition. By treating hallucinations as geometric phenomena rather than semantic deviations, GHT provides a structural foundation for interpretability, safety, and the design of future geometric AI architectures. It positions hallucinations within the broader framework of structural AI, where models are understood as dynamical geometric objects rather than probabilistic text generators. The taxonomy serves both as a research contribution and as a navigational map of the geometric‑AI system it documents. --- Relation to Prior Work This preprint serves as an independent, external interpretive supplement to the geometric‑operator framework introduced in: Marín, J. (2026). A geometric taxonomy of hallucinations in large language models. arXiv:2602.13224. It is not authored by, endorsed by, or affiliated with the authors of that work. Instead, it extends the geometric‑operator perspective by providing a structural taxonomy of hallucination modes grounded in curvature, spectral dynamics, holonomy, topology, and nonlinear fusion‑field operators. ---

Notably, we employ five algorithms for performance comparison. We also investigate the propagation of faults from a framework to its downstream dependency applications (100 applications) in Machine Learning (ML) and non-ML domain across Java and Python programming language. We are motivated to carry out this study because of the ever-growing integration of LLM into modern software application so that quality of such application is kept up-to-date optimally from the angle of fault localization and fault propagation. Next, we evaluate our approach on existing baseline fault localization techniques on baseline datasets (Defects4J and Tests4Py) in which our result outperforms the best existing techniques on the baselines. Furthermore, we evaluate our approach with stand-alone Claude reasoning model on baseline datasets (Defects4J and Tests4Py) and we found that the Top-1 prediction of our approach outperforms Claude's Top-1 prediction. Hence, we justify our study applicability to real-world scenarios. We provide the step-wise approach of our implementation below.
