documents.abstract: Clinical biochemistry generates approximately 70% of the objective data used in medical decision-making, yet the integration of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, and large language models (LLMs) into laboratory operations remains fragmented. Existing digital-health maturity constructs (HIMSS EMRAM, HITI, CAMM) do not jointly address analytical metrology, algorithmic lifecycle governance, and clinical outcome accountability, leaving laboratories without a structured roadmap for AI-augmented diagnostic stewardship. To develop and face-validate the biochemistry–AI Stewardship Maturity (BASM) framework, a system-level maturity model that links laboratory analytics, AI governance, and health-service outcomes across five progressive tiers. A PRISMA-ScR-guided scoping review of six databases (MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, Cochrane) covering January 2022–July 2026 identified 1,482 records; 29 sources were retained after dual-independent screening (Cohen’s κ = 0.86). Charted evidence was triangulated with IFCC, ADLM, CAP, and CLSI position statements, and consolidated into a seven-dimension rubric. Face validity was assessed with five laboratory directors, and structural comparisons were performed against four precedent maturity models. BASM operationalizes maturity across seven dimensions—analytical foundations, data infrastructure, algorithmic lifecycle governance, diagnostic stewardship, workforce competency, equity and safety, and outcome accountability—resolved into five ordinal tiers (BASM-1 to BASM-5) with 12–24-month transition milestones. A chain of custody aggregation rule prevents high analytical scores from masking governance or equity deficits. Alignment with TRIPOD + AI, DECIDE-AI, and TRIPOD-LLM reporting standards is embedded at tiers 3–5. BASM provides laboratories, health systems, and regulators with an actionable, standards-aligned instrument to plan, benchmark, and audit AI-augmented diagnostic stewardship. A multi-institutional modified-Delphi validation is the priority next step.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled clinical decision support systems (CDSSs) increasingly combine structured clinical data and medical images, but their explanations differ in cost, format, storage, and failure behavior. This study presents a modality-adaptive software architecture for a browser-based CDSS supporting 10-year coronary heart disease (CHD) prediction, 30-day hospital readmission prediction, and chest-radiograph classification with 14 independent output scores. The architecture treats explanation selection as a request-time service policy: Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) accompany tabular predictions; local interpretable model-agnostic explanations (LIME) are requested separately; gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) and its generalized variant (Grad-CAM++) are computed only for threshold-positive classes within the five highest-ranked scores; and large language model (LLM) narratives are attempted when configured. React, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, and a seven-day Redis cache implement the design. Seven synthetic fixture families satisfied the specified selection conditions. In a backend experiment involving 7,818 radiographs, heatmap generation averaged 140.2 ms per radiograph, or 78.2% of the 179.3-ms mean total. A separate in-process service-layer test completed all 3,600 requests successfully using deterministic prediction and explanation substitutes and SQLite persistence. The architecture specifies bounded explanation work and separate retention paths. Full-stack performance, clinical-model calibration, explanation quality, and clinician benefit remain subjects for future evaluation.

documents.abstract: This article analyzes the effects of GAI- Generative Artificial Intelligence- on contemporary forms of perception, language, and symbolic connection. Based on an interdisciplinary approach—drawing from philosophy, semiotics, and sociology—the study explores the collapse of critical and sensitive perception amidst the informational saturation of digital media, particularly in the context of the so-called “dead internet.” Using Generation Z as a paradigmatic expression of a new cultural sensibility, the paper discusses the transformation of authorship regimes, the dissolution of the public sphere, and the blurred boundaries between human and machine in meaning-making processes. This research investigates inflection points between classical models of reason and emerging aesthetic experiences shaped by technology. In the midst of symbolic emptiness, the concept of re-enchantment of the world (Maffesoli) is presented as a potential response—restoring presence, shared language, and affective bonds. The analysis seeks to foster a critical reflection on the role of culture, ethics, and communication in mediating the impacts of artificial intelligence, and emphasizes the urgency of symbolic reconfiguration in an era of perceptual collapse.

Abstract. Wind and solar energy are two popular alternative energy sources. However, wind turbines are larger and more complex than solar panels. Accordingly, wind turbines are more exposed to environmental factors and therefore more prone to mechanical failures. Our work improves the reliability and efficiency of wind energy systems by presenting an artificial intelligence (AI)-based system that predicts mechanical gearbox and electrical failures. Historical data are aggregated with real-time sensor data to train the prediction model. Apart from related mechanical and environmental data, sensors provide real-time vibration, internal nacelle temperature, wind speed, noise and smoke levels. The developed system integrates AI and Large Language Model (LLM)-based interfaces for real-time interactive monitoring of turbines. The user interface of the developed system allows users to receive informative responses on performance, detected risks, predicted failures, and energy production levels. The developed model has been validated using 5-fold cross-validation based on Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-Score, and ROC-AUC. The model achieves approximately 89.68 % Accuracy, 90.08 % F1- Score, 95.65 % ROC-AUC, and novel metric 65.13 %, Overall Performance. The performance results demonstrate the promising potential of AI- and LLM-integrated systems for wind energy applications. Prototype data, labeled via the XGBoost model trained with SCADA data, was retrained using the LightGBM algorithm, achieving 98.37 % Accuracy, 99.16 % F1-Score, 98.95 % ROC-AUC and 94.65 % Overall Performance; the analysis proved that the newly added gas and sound sensors significantly improved the fault prediction performance of the system.

Abstract While Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable zero-shot learning capabilities, their deployment in real-time interactive systems is constrained by sparse terminal feedback in long-sequence generation, unstable policy updates, and the computational overhead associated with verbose outputs. To address these challenges, this paper formalizes autoregressive text generation as a discrete-time Markov decision process (MDP) and proposes a latency-aware composite reward optimization framework based on proximal policy optimization (PPO). The core contribution of the proposed method is a multidimensional sequence-level terminal reward that jointly evaluates semantic coherence, lexical diversity, and computational cost. Specifically, a Natural Language Inference (NLI) cross-encoder evaluates the semantic consistency between the input context and the complete generated response, while Shannon entropy and Distinct-N metrics encourage lexical diversity. In addition, a hardware-aware penalty based on generated sequence length and measured inference latency discourages unnecessarily verbose outputs and promotes computationally efficient generation. During policy optimization, the terminal composite reward is propagated through generalized advantage estimation, while a token-wise Kullback–Leibler divergence term regularizes the updated policy against the reference policy. This formulation does not introduce token-level semantic rewards; instead, it combines informative sequence-level evaluation with step-wise policy regularization to improve empirical training stability. We evaluated the proposed framework on a large-scale hybrid corpus containing approximately 320,000 dialogue turns, including real-world English interaction data. Compared with the standard PPO baseline, the proposed method exhibited faster empirical convergence and lower variability in the observed training trajectories. It achieved a BLEU-4 score of 22.87 and a Distinct-2 score of 21.59%, while reducing the average inference latency to 42.8 milliseconds per token under the reported hardware configuration. These results demonstrate the potential of latency-aware composite reward optimization to balance response quality, lexical diversity, and inference efficiency in real-time domain-specific LLM applications.

We formulate a common discrete configuration space in which edge lengths encode piecewise-flat geometry, a causal orientation defines a partial order, and compact gauge holonomies on the same oriented edges represent the local gauge group of the Standard Model. A single formal configuration sum combines a four-dimensional Regge gravitational action, Wilson-type gauge actions, a Higgs sector, and a chiral matter sector. We derive the local gauge-transformation laws and show that face-trace actions are gauge invariant. We state a conditional stability result for a finite Euclidean edge regulator and explain why it does not establish stability of the full Lorentzian gravitational path integral. On a regular-lattice regulator, the standard low-momentum lattice dispersion is recovered as a calculation within the regulator, not as a prediction of the irregular dynamical network. The Newtonian limit is recovered conditionally if the geometry sum has a continuum phase governed by the Einstein–Hilbert action. This construction is a synthesis/ansatz, not a demonstrated Theory of Everything: the measure over complexes, the chiral lattice fermion operator, renormalized continuum limit, and a derivation of the Standard Model parameters remain unresolved. The common carrier of interactions should not be confused with unification of their couplings or symmetries. Acknowledgements: The author expresses gratitude to family, peers, and independent researchers for technical feedback on the mathematical infrastructure. Computational synthesis, linguistic polishing, and manuscript structural formatting assistance were supported by large language model AI assistants (Gemini and ChatGPT).

Biobank-scale imaging-genomic cohorts enable genome-wide association studies (GWASs) of organ structure and function. Traditional approaches rely on expert-defined image-derived phenotypes (IDPs), which capture only a fraction of the biological variation in high-content images. Powered by artificial intelligence, self-supervised learning (SSL) learns representations directly from intrinsic image structures, creating scalable, data-driven traits. Here, we review the technical frameworks and challenges of SSL-based imaging genetics and their applications in brain MRI, cardiac MRI, and retinal imaging. Early studies suggest that these data-driven approaches can complement traditional IDPs and may expand the phenotypic space available for discovery of heritable imaging traits, although broader validation across cohorts, ancestries, scanners, and imaging protocols remains needed.

documents.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly used in software development for coding, debugging, documentation, and learning. This study examines its adoption, benefits, challenges, security concerns, dependence, learning support, and future impact. Survey responses from 21 programming students and professionals were analyzed using frequencies, percentages, and average ratings. Of the respondents, 95.2% reported daily or frequent use and 95.2% used ChatGPT. Debugging and error fixing was the most common task (71.4%). Respondents reported benefits such as better problem-solving and faster development, but also identified bugs, security issues, architectural complexity, and privacy concerns. Overall, GenAI is viewed as a useful assistant, but human review, testing, and responsible use remain essential. The findings are exploratory due to the small sample size.

Data storage and processing have been fundamentally changed with the advent of cloud computing, which offers options for accessing computing resources with a certain level of flexibility and depends on the scale. However, this convenience provides a lot of room for security vulnerabilities where attackers can compromise systems, exfiltrate personal information, and, in many cases, the most pressing security threats are posed by individuals who have access to the corporate infrastructure legitimately. To counteract such problems, enterprises use multi-layered security architecture. Rather than just using a password as authentication, modern systems require multi-factor authentication, which can be any combination of a password and a text message containing a one-time password, a biometric scan, or both. Once you have access, policies are in place concerning what you are allowed to do, and organizations will often assign specific, discrete roles like manager or employee to different types of users associated with certain levels of permission and access. Authorization models are often followed like role-based access control (RBAC) and attribute-based access control (ABAC), which explicitly specify user privileges inside cloud environments. The world of cloud security has witnessed an exponential growth in recent years, as organizations are using increasingly more artificial intelligence (AI)-based solutions to identify anomalous behaviors that may indicate an imminent attack. The hegemonic “never trust, always verify” paradigm has taken root in the realm of the cloud, carefully checking every request before giving access or permission to the same, regardless of its origin. Implementing these safeguards is not only important to thwarting attacks but to meeting basic requirements in protecting sensitive information, preventing unauthorized modification, and ensuring continuity in the event of incidences, thus providing data privacy. Finally, organizations are legally and industry required to meet various standards for the protection of customer data, further making it a complex task to plan and implement effective cloud security strategies.

Fatal railway level crossing crashes represent a public safety challenge. Existing data on these crashes is limited, mostly focusing on frequencies rather than providing an in-depth understanding of the underlying causes. This study aimed to demonstrate the utility of using coronial findings, supplemented with reports from investigation agencies, to understand the system-wide factors contributing to railway crossing crashes and to explore the proposed recommendations. A systems thinking accident analysis approach, the AcciMap technique, underpinned the analysis. Over a 20-year period, 151 cases were identified, involving a range of road user types. Of these cases, 135 included sufficient detail to extract contributory factors and recommendations. A total of 483 contributory factors were extracted and used to develop an aggregate AcciMap. Most factors were associated with road user behaviour and/or individual characteristics, as opposed to systemic issues. Unique contributory factors were identified for crashes occurring at active crossings (those with dynamic warnings present) versus passive crossings (those with signage only). A total of 184 recommendations were extracted and mapped using the AcciMap framework. Recommendations tended to take a system-wide view of preventing future occurrences, acknowledging the complexity of managing risk at the interface of two transport modes. The analysis provided important information to support crash prevention efforts, including a set of common systemic recommendations identified from the data that require collaborative efforts across road and rail stakeholders. Mechanisms for supporting this collaboration should be further explored. The study also provided learnings regarding the nature of coronial investigations and areas for potential improvement.

Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a common neurotype experienced among children and adolescents worldwide. Students with ADHD often face challenges with academic motivation and achievement which impacts their academic achievement at school. Factors contributing to these challenges include difficulty with sustaining attention, planning and organisation of tasks and activities, and time management. At school, students with ADHD experience challenges initiating learning tasks, particularly those of which they are not interested or are perceived to be overwhelming to start. Students with ADHD who lack motivation to start and engage in learning activities decrease their ability to remain on task resulting in disengagement from learning. Lower academic achievement in school is linked to poorer educational attainment (e.g., fewer years spent in compulsory schooling or post-secondary education) and occupational outcomes (e.g., lower income, higher unemployment) for individuals with ADHD post schooling. This systematic review explores the role of academic motivation on academic achievement among students with ADHD. The review identified a paucity of research with only three published papers (representing two independent samples), published between 2020 and 2023, meeting the inclusion criteria. Findings showed that both amotivation and cognitively challenging task motivation negatively predicted grade point average. Results also found that extrinsic and intrinsic motivation positively predicted academic outcomes. These findings indicate that supporting the academic achievement of students with ADHD is critically important for learning and academic success at school. These data also expand this important area of research beyond formal schooling to higher education and the workplace to ensure that students with ADHD continue to realise successful university and career outcomes. Additionally, future research could explore the role of extrinsic motivation as a strategy to support academic achievement among those with ADHD, or act as a stepping stone toward developing more intrinsically oriented forms of motivation.

Minority and underserved youth are less likely to undergo diabetic retinopathy screening, yet more likely to have diabetic retinopathy. We hypothesize that autonomous artificial intelligence-based diabetic eye exams could mitigate screening disparities in minority youth. This prospective study enrolled 397 White and non-White youth with type 1 (72%) and type 2 (28%) diabetes at diabetes care visits. Participants underwent autonomous artificial-intelligence diabetic eye exams and optical coherence tomography imaging. The primary outcome is equivalence in screening completion between White and non-White youth. The secondary outcome is diagnostic accuracy of AI against prognostic standard. At baseline, participants in the White cohort were more likely to have completed a prior diabetic eye exam (79.8% v 61.8%, p < 0.0001). Following the artificial-intelligence intervention, 99.5% in the White cohort and 98% in the non-White cohort completed the autonomous artificial-intelligence diabetic eye exam, demonstrating equivalent screening completion after implementation. When compared to standard grading, AI demonstrated sensitivity of 100% (95% CI: 67.6%, 100%), and specificity of 76% (95% CI: 71.4%, 79.9%) for detecting more than mild diabetic retinopathy. Implementation of autonomous AI at the point of care increases access to and completion of diabetic eye exams, achieving equivalent screening completion among White and non-White youth, suggesting the potential to reduce disparities in diabetic retinopathy screening. Study Registration: NCT05463289. This study demonstrates that autonomous AI screening for diabetic retinopathy can achieve equivalent screening completion among white and non-white youth with T1D, suggesting the potential to reduce disparities in diabetic retinopathy screening.

Large language models serve applications with diverse inference budgets, but training and maintaining separate models for each budget incurs substantial costs. Recent Looped Transformers enable flexible inference computation through parameter reuse, but maintaining strong performance across different inference budgets remains an open challenge. We introduce Accordion, a mixture-of-experts-based model that supports five inference budgets through fixed-prefix layer looping. Each budget follows a pre-defined execution path, while the minimum budget retains the unlooped model. Joint pretraining samples one budget per micro-batch and optimizes its next-token prediction loss without additional cross-budget consistency objectives. We further preserve these inference budgets through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, where parameter-group merging and budget-matched multi-teacher on-policy distillation integrate three domain experts into one model. After 3.6T tokens of pretraining, increasing inference depth improves Accordion-6B-A0.5B's five-category macro-average across 37 tasks by 3.01 percentage points, with the middle budget capturing 89% of this gain using half as many additional layer executions. The final model surpasses each domain expert on its corresponding task-and-budget average, while achieving strong instruction-following performance across all budgets and retaining depth-dependent gains in mathematical reasoning and code generation.

Purpose – Business researchers can address climate challenges by developing solutions with high social impact. This study aims to propose a framework for how business researchers can shift their focus from theory development to contribute also practical solutions that increase the social impact of their work. Design/methodology/approach – Drawing on prior literature and concepts related to creating social impact for climate change mitigation, the authors categorise current business research on pro-environmental behaviours into Mode 1 and Mode 2. Mode 1 focuses on theory development. Mode 2 emphasises practical implications. This study covers a wide range of pro-environmental behaviours across various business contexts. Findings – The framework developed identifies five key factors that determine the social impact of business research: leveraging foundational theoretical knowledge, testing the impact of newly proposed solutions in field studies, measuring actual outcomes, collaborating with industry and policymakers and working across scholarly disciplines. Originality/value – This framework offers business researchers guidance on designing Mode 2 research to maximise social impact. This framework serves as an essential resource for business researchers aiming to translate their theoretical knowledge into practical solutions.

LLM agents need long-term memory that can recover precise and mutually consistent evidence from growing interaction histories, particularly when answers depend on relations among facts rather than isolated semantic matches. Current memory pipelines remain vulnerable at two stages: indexing errors can fragment repeated entities or merge distinct ones, and online retrieval often treats initial similarity scores as final even when the surrounding graph provides evidence for revising them. We introduce ActionRAG, a graph memory architecture that couples cautious indexing with query-time graph retroevaluation. Its indexing pipeline reconciles type labels and applies tiered entity resolution. Given a query, dual-channel entity and triple retrieval forms an initial evidence set and induces a bounded local graph. Query-conditioned receiver-normalized diffusion refines triple scores using local path structure. Seed protection, hub-penalized flux, and triple materialization preserve direct evidence while recovering missed connections. We evaluate ActionRAG on MemoryAgentBench (MAB), which tests accurate retrieval, conflict resolution, long-range understanding, and test-time learning. Across its eight deterministic-scoring columns, ActionRAG achieves 55.1 average accuracy, improving over the strongest retrieval-based memory baseline by 5.4 points. Under MAB's query-time cost accounting, mean synthesis cost stays below \$0.001 per query on the four reported cost columns, and the sum of separately measured retrieval-side p99 components is 440.7 ms on our consumer Apple Silicon setup.

Abstract We develop an active inference route-planning method for autonomous control of an intelligent agent. The aim is to reconnoiter a geographical area while balancing search and tracking behaviors to maintain a dynamic situational awareness map. To achieve this, we construct an evidence map that reflects our current understanding of the situation, integrating both positive and “negative” sensor observations of possible target objects collected over time, and diffusing the evidence across the map as time progresses. The generative model of active inference uses Dempster-Shafer theory and a Gaussian sensor model to provide input to the agent. The generative process employs a Bayesian approach to update a posterior probability distribution. We calculate the variational free energy across all locations within the sensor radius by assessing the divergence between a pignistic probability distribution of the evidence map and a posterior probability distribution of the target object, including the level of surprisal associated with receiving new observations. Using the variational free energy, we direct the agent’s movement in simulation by taking incremental steps toward a position that minimizes the variational free energy. This approach addresses the challenge of balancing exploration and exploitation, allowing the agent to search large areas while efficiently tracking identified targets. Across 1000 simulation trials, the approach surpasses benchmarks in target observation by an average of 51%–69% across various metrics for a 100-meter sensor radius.

Autonomous and semi-autonomous AI agents now plan, call tools, change records and delegate work to other agents at machine speed. Most enterprise controls assume a human decides and a deterministic application executes, so they do not cover this. The Agentic Defence and Assurance Model (ADAM) is a proposed operational framework for governing, securing and assuring AI agents in the enterprise. Its foundational proposition is that autonomy must never exceed accountability. ADAM has three architectural dimensions. Governance and Accountability sets the conditions under which agents may operate. Six Operational Security Layers (PREVENT, CONSTRAIN, DETECT, INTERRUPT, RECOVER and REVALIDATE) provide the runtime controls. Continuous Assurance and Evidence demonstrates that those controls work. Four capabilities cut across all six layers: agent identity, delegated authority, independent enforcement and operational telemetry. The report also introduces several proposed constructs: the Agent Autonomy Envelope, a four-tier agent risk classification, a catalogue of 29 controls, a six-point maturity scale with three separate assessment dimensions, and two exploratory metrics. ADAM is designed to complement NIST, ISO/IEC, OWASP and MITRE resources, not to replace them. Version 0.1 is published for comment. This record contains the technical report (PDF), the framework diagrams (PDF and editable SVG), the briefing presentation (PDF) and the control catalogue (CSV).

Abstract Graph neural networks (GNNs) have emerged as an effective framework for biological sequence classification using De Bruijn graphs, yet node representations have received comparatively less attention. Although multiscale Expected Density of Nucleotide (EDN) provides informative sequence-level representations, it cannot be directly incorporated into graph-based sequence learning because De Bruijn graphs require node-level representations. To address this challenge, we propose Contextual Multiscale Expected Density of Nucleotide (cMSEDN), a lightweight, deterministic framework that adapts multiscale EDN sequence representations into sequence-specific node embeddings for De Bruijn graph learning while preserving k-mer identity and incorporating occurrence-level context. Unlike static k-mer encodings, cMSEDN aggregates occurrence-level contextual features so that identical k-mers can receive distinct sequence-specific representations across different biological sequences. We evaluated the proposed framework on seven biological sequence classification datasets spanning transcription factor binding prediction, promoter recognition, and RNA subcellular localization across multiple species, and encompassing both DNA and RNA sequence analysis tasks using GCN and GIN architectures. Compared with conventional context-independent node representations, off-the-shelf foundation models serving as static node-feature extractors, and a static EDN-based baseline, cMSEDN consistently achieved improved classification performance across the benchmark suite for De Bruijn Graph Neural Networks while using compact deterministic embeddings. These results indicate that our sequence-specific k -mer encoding is an effective, computationally lightweight bio-sequence graph representation for sequence classification, requiring no modifications to the underlying GNN architecture.
